#2683. James sees a lot to like — and improve — for East-leading Sixers

James sees a lot to like — and improve — for East-leading Sixers originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

LeBron James likes to refer to the NBA season as a "marathon."

A few miles in, the Sixers lead the Eastern Conference pack.

With 17 regular-season contests down of 82, the team sits at 14-3, which is 2.5 games ahead of the second-seeded Celtics. The Sixers squeaked out their latest win, a 132-129 decision Saturday over the cellar-dwelling Bucks, but the bottom line is they've become accustomed to finding many routes to victory.

"We want to build habits," James said. "We want to try to take steps forward every game that we get the opportunity. I know sometimes it doesn't happen that way, but we want to do it.

"We want to strive to be as great as we can offensively, defensively and on special teams. A win is a win, but there's ways to win and ways to try to continue to build habits over the course of a marathon."

All sorts of Sixers games have gone down to the wire and they've won every single one.

The team is an incredible 12-0 in clutch situations, defined as games with a point differential of five or under in the final five minutes. The Sixers rank third in the NBA in clutch offensive rating (140.3) and third in clutch net rating (plus-42.0).

"It's good to build that part of our game," James said. "Obviously, we wanted to close the game out a lot better. But a team like that, we know they're going to be scrappy. They're going to play as hard as they can for 48 minutes. … We can learn from that."

James was the centerpiece of the Sixers' fourth-quarter offense Saturday. He scored 13 of his 21 points between the 7:46 and 3:13 mark of the fourth.

The four-time MVP got two buckets on no-nonsense drives and another on an after-timeout isolation hoop over rookie Brayden Burries. James also scored three times on a designed Horns action where he brought the ball up, used Tyrese Maxey's back screen at the elbow and caused serious problems for Milwaukee in the paint.

"We continue to add things to the half-court offense and also to the late-game package," Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said. "That's something we added a few game ago. It's one of those things where, especially if we're in the bonus, we've got some big bodies that can cut down the lane and have feel for timing. It was working. Just keep going to it."

James has grown in comfort with Nurse's coaching style. He knows the Sixers expect him to be a de facto coach on the floor, too.

"I'm just trying to be there for the team in any capacity they want," he said. "Just trying to be an extension of his calls and his commands out there on the floor. Trying to make his life and his job a little bit easier as well.

"But it's been great, not only with him but the whole coaching staff. They've welcomed me with open arms and allowed me to kind of be the voice for the team every day, and take that responsibility."

After a tremendous first impression defensively and some subpar offensive nights, the Sixers' numbers have recently evened out.

The team is 12th in offensive rating outside of garbage time and 12th in defensive rating, per Cleaning the Glass. In essence, the Sixers have been a bit above average on both ends of the floor and downright brilliant in the closing minutes.

It's all added up to an early lead in a very long race.

"I think we've bought into the pass," James said. "We have so many guys that can score the ball at elite levels. … In order for us to be a super-complete team, I think the power of the pass is very infectious. And it's also key for our other guys, to make sure they feel in a rhythm and they feel confident. We've done that from Day 1 and I think it's gotten better and better. … And I think our defense has been really good for the majority of the season.

"(Today) it wasn't so great, but we've been very good defensively throughout the course of the season. … I don't want to say there's anything bad. There's so many things for us to do better for sure. There's games where we can defensive rebound a lot better and there's games where we can not turn the ball over (as much). And there's games where we can be a little more phsyical defensively at the point of attack like (today).

"I wouldn't say anything has been bad, though. That's a good thing. We want to continue to have room for improvement and we don't want to be great in November. That would be weird."

#2681. Max Verstappen Spent 40 Hours Playing GTA VI in Las Vegas Before Winning Saturday's Grand Prix

Max Verstappen found an unusual way to spend his free time during the Las Vegas Grand Prix weekend. The Red Bull driver revealed that he played GTA VI for more than 40 hours before winning Saturday's race.

Speaking during a gaming livestream in the days after the race, Verstappen shared how much time he had spent playing the new game. "40 hours. I played a lot in the evening and the morning in Vegas," he revealed. He also explained that staying inside gave him time to play.

The timing made his gaming marathon even more surprising. GTA VI launched on November 19, just as F1 arrived in Las Vegas for its race weekend. Verstappen fitted gaming sessions around his practice, qualifying, and race commitments.

Despite spending so much time in the virtual world, Verstappen delivered another strong performance on track. He started from pole position and led most of the 50-lap race. The victory marked his third win in Las Vegas and fourth of the 2026 season.

Verstappen found another reason to compare Formula 1 with video games after winning the Las Vegas Grand Prix. The Red Bull driver likened the race's constant passing and repassing to Nintendo's Mario Kart.

Max Verstappen was reminded of video game racing amid a chaotic Las Vegas GP. (Source: MEGA)

The 50-lap race featured a total of 352 overtakes and 35 changes of the lead. The Dutchman repeatedly lost first place on the back straight (the Vegas Strip) before fighting back at the next series of corners in the run to the finish line. He said the experience reminded him of the catch-up effect in Mario Kart.

Gaming has long been part of Verstappen's life away from the circuit. The four-time world champion regularly competes in online sim racing events and has his own racing simulator at home. He also races with Team Redline, a professional sim racing team.

Video games remain a crucial part of Max Verstappen's life. (Source: MEGA)

Earlier in 2026, Verstappen even joked that he had swapped his simulator for a Nintendo Switch. He made the comment while discussing the new F1 cars and their heavy focus on battery management. His latest GTA VI marathon in Las Vegas offered another glimpse into his gaming interests.

Verstappen was not the only F1 driver excited about Grand Theft Auto VI during the Las Vegas Grand Prix weekend. Lewis Hamilton also brought his PlayStation and planned to spend his free time playing the game. He called it "the most anticipated game ever" and admitted, "I'm like a big kid."

Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli had already pre-ordered and downloaded the game. He even asked his father to bring his PlayStation to the circuit. Isack Hadjar also found time for around 25 minutes of gameplay before heading to the track.

Other drivers also shared their interest in the release. George Russell watched gameplay videos, while Pierre Gasly regretted leaving his gaming laptop at home. Alex Albon also wished he had brought a portable console to Las Vegas as well.

However, not everyone was equally excited. Lando Norris revealed that his parents had banned him from playing GTA as a child. Valtteri Bottas also had other plans, saying he preferred spending his free time outdoors.

#2677. How the Sixers can advance to the NBA Cup knockout round

The Joel Embiid-less Sixers got pasted Monday by the Portland Trail Blazers, but they have a golden opportunity to wash that bad taste out of their mouths. Their next two games are their final two games in the NBA Cup's group-play stage, and they still aren't eliminated from earning a spot in the knockout round.

Here's a glimpse at the current standings heading into Wednesday's games:

And here's a reminder of how the tiebreakers work, which very well could come into play to determine the winner of East Group B:

Point differential in group play (not including overtime)

Total points scored in group play (not including overtime)

Random drawing if none of those tiebreakers resolve the tie

It might look like the Heat are sitting pretty at 2-0 with a plus-32 point differential, but they face the Sixers on Wednesday and the New York Knicks on Friday. There's a non-zero chance they're 2-2 by the end of that stretch, which would likely end their chances of winning Group B.

So, what do the Sixers need to emerge as the winners of Group B? First, they have to sweep the Heat and Pacers this week. Anything short of a 3-1 record will all but guarantee their elimination.

Even if they do win both games, the Cleveland Cavaliers are lurking as a roadblock since the Cavs have the head-to-head tiebreaker over them. The Sixers would need the Knicks to beat the Cavs on Wednesday, which would push them down to 2-2.

If the Knicks do beat the Cavs and the Sixers beat both the Heat and Pacers, they will win Group B and advance to the knockout round. If the Sixers beat both the Heat and Pacers but the Cavs beat the Knicks, the Cavs will win Group B, and the Sixers will have to hope to sneak into the knockout round with a wild-card spot.

The Sixers' minus-19 point differential won't help them in the wild-card race, though. They'll need to run up the score against both the Heat and Pacers to give themselves a realistic chance of securing a wild-card bid.

If the Sixers fall short of the knockout round, it once and for all proves that they're frauds this year, obviously. They'll also have two games added to their schedule between Dec. 6-10 based on a "formulaic approach" that uses the group-play standings in each conference, according to the NBA.

"Two of the 22 games will be scheduled cross-conference since there will be an odd number of teams in each conference that do not advance to the quarterfinals. These cross-conference games will be scheduled between bottom- finishing teams in the Group Play stage subject to travel constraints, and no team will play more than one of its two games cross-conference. The other 20 games will be scheduled within conference featuring teams that are otherwise scheduled to play each other three times over the course of the season wherever possible."

The Sixers have never advanced to the knockout round of the NBA Cup yet, and they're facing an uphill battle to get there this year thanks to their blowout loss to the Cavs. But they aren't dead yet, especially if they beat the Heat on Wednesday and the Cavs lose to the Knicks.

So, as you gather round your family for the holidays this week, be sure to tell them what really matters: Sweating NBA Cup games on Thanksgiving Eve.

Against the Kings they shot 33.7% from the field and 22.4% on threes. Against the Warriors, they shot 38.6% from the field and 29.8% from beyond the arc. It may be fatigue or the travel or just a lack of focus, but they have to get their focus back on taking good shots and making them. They are struggling especially on threes but yet they keep shooting, and missing, them. X-FactorsOn the Road and Fatigue – The Celtics are playing in the final game of a 4 game road trip. The last game of a road trip is always hard to win. They are also playing in the 3rd game in 4 nights so fatigue may come into play. They have to overcome the distractions that come with playing on the road like travel, missing family, an unfamiliar building and a hostile crowd. They have to stay focused on playing Celtics basketball the right way and not on the crowd, the court, or the Wizards' record.

Officiating -Officiating is always an x-factor in every game. Every crew officiates differently. Some call it tight, others let them play. Some favor the home team. Some favor the road team. Some just make bad, head scratching calls. The Celtics need to adjust to how the refs are calling the game and not allow bad calls or no calls to take away their focus on playing the game.

#2671. Dan Quinn on Stefon Diggs: I love his fire

#2669. Geno Auriemma at a loss after UConn’s loss to rival South Carolina: ‘I have to figure it out’

UNCASVILLE, Conn. — After spending the majority of his career making opposing coaches uncomfortable, legendary UConn coach Geno Auriemma met his match.

Dawn Staley's Gamecocks, the No. 1 team in the country, delivered a tough lesson to No. 7 UConn on Tuesday.

Auriemma was as despondent as he's been all season following UConn's 65-56 loss that dropped the Huskies to 4-3 on the season.

"You might be able to tell that and I'm having a really hard time coaching this team, and I have to figure it out," Auriemma said. "But it'd be nice if I got a little help."

Auriemma seemed embarrassed after losing to No. 5 Michigan by 11 on Nov. 5. He was annoyed when UConn fell to No. 7 Louisville, 69-51, a week and a half later.

Geno Auriemma talks to center Olivia Vukosa (second from left) during UConn's 65-56 loss to South Carolina on Nov. 24, 2026, in Uncasville, Conn. AP

But Auriemma had no explanation for what transpired against the Gamecocks, a team that should bring out the best in his group.

"It's already hard enough to beat the best team in the country when you are actually beating yourself," Auriemma said. "It's incredibly frustrating and just at a loss. Usually I have a pretty good idea but …"

He questioned his team's mental toughness.

The final score may suggest a competitive game. But the second quarter told the real story of the night.

The Huskies, playing without KK Arnold and Kayleigh Heckel, won the first quarter, 16-11. But the Gamecocks took over and never looked back while winning for the seventh time in the past 10 meetings of this rivalry.

South Carolina upped its defensive intensity and started hitting shots. UConn fouled too much, missed layups and allowed Tessa Johnson and Agot Makeer to get hot from deep in that second quarter.

The Gamecocks, despite being without Joyce Edwards (sickness), outscored UConn 27-6 in the second quarter and went on a 15-0 run to close the first half and lead by 16 at halftime.

Johnson scored 32 points, surpassing her career high she set earlier this month in the Gamecocks' win against No. 3 USC.

Geno Auriemma and Dawn Staley shake hands before South Carolina's road victory over UConn. AP

"It feels great to get a win," Staley said. "And it feels super great for a player like Tessa who works extremely hard. What you're seeing is a product of a player that is always in the gym."

Players would like you to believe that South Carolina-UConn is just another game. But Tuesday added another layer in one of college basketball's greatest rivalries.

"It feels good," said Ashlyn Watkins, who stepped up in a big way in Edwards' absence. "It's still early in the season, so we're going to see them again, probably, but we're ready for sure."

Tuesday was the first meeting since Auriemma and Staley's fiery sideline spat in the final seconds of South Carolina's national semifinal win in April.

The two hadn't spoken since the incident, Auriemma told reporters Sunday.

Tessa Johnson, who scored a career-high 32 points, shoots a jumper over Ashlynn Shade during South Carolina's road win over UConn. David Butler II-Imagn Images

The two didn't appear to exchange words pregame or postgame Tuesday.

They did, however, share a brief handshake before and after the game.

This past weekend, Auriemma did his best to downplay any lingering hostility toward Staley.

"I don't coach against other coaches," Auriemma told reporters. "I coach against their players."

But there has to be something about beating a fierce rival that makes a win so much more satisfying, right?

"We play UConn enough to where it is just a game," Staley said. "It's a big game but we've played them enough to where we understand the gravity of the game, we understand the NCAA committee implications and all that goes into it. … But other than that, whether we won or lost, it's not gonna impact us in a way that, like, we're gonna get better, no matter what at this stage of the game. We're not gonna be the team that took the floor today in March or February.

"So it's always good to see how we measure up to a UConn team that's always at the top of the game."

#2667. Joel Embiid doubtful for Sixers’ NBA Cup showdown vs. Miami Heat

The Sixers are getting dangerously close to full strength, which means in true Sixers fashion, calamity is right around the corner. Lo and behold, Joel Embiid came down with an illness that caused him to miss Monday's game against the Portland Trail Blazers, and he's still dealing with it a day later.

Embiid is doubtful to suit up for the Sixers' NBA Cup game against the Miami Heat on Wednesday, according to the NBA's injury report. The good news is that aside from Embiid and Ariel Hukporti (Achilles), no one else is even listed for the Sixers. So much for Jaylen Brown's hamstring injury!

On Miami's side, two-way signees Tre Donaldson and Vladislav Goldin are out on assignment in the G League, while Myron Gardner is available. The big question mark is Giannis Antetokounmpo, who's listed as questionable with right groin tendinitis. He missed Miami's win over the Oklahoma City Thunder on Sunday with the same injury, and in his absence, Bam Adebayo messed around and got a triple-double.

If Giannis is able to suit up and Embiid misses the game, the Sixers will have a hell of a time stopping him and Bam down low. None of Jabari Walker, Dominick Barlow or Adem Bona have the size to combat the Greek Freak in transition. But if Giannis does sit out, it'll be more of a fair fight.

The Heat sit atop East Group B with a 2-0 record, while the Sixers are 1-1. If the Heat beat the Sixers, they'll be all but guaranteed to win the group, as they'll have the head-to-head tiebreaker over both the Sixers and Cleveland Cavaliers. But if the Embiid-less Sixers can take down the Heat, they'll have a chance to win Group B as long as the New York Knicks beat the Cavs later Wednesday.

The Sixers have never advanced to the knockout stage of the NBA Cup, but they've also never had NBA Cup MVP LeBron James on their roster before this year. And since LeBron is playing on a veteran-minimum contract this year, the prize money for winning the Cup would be more than 10 percent of his salary. That's assuredly a huge motivation for someone with an estimated net worth of $1.4 billion.

Embiid's likely absence will give the Sixers a chance to continue experimenting with their backup options as they inch closer to the start of unofficial trade season. They largely went with a Walker-Barlow combo against the Blazers—Bona played only five minutes in his first game back from a cervical spine sprain—but it's worth keeping an eye on whether the Sixers change that up against the Heat. They should still be in the intel-gathering stage of the season, so the more they mix it up, the better. (Could we even get some brief Tacko Time?)

As someone whose two-year-old is just getting over hand, foot and mouth disease, it's that time of the year for parents. Here's hoping the rest of the Sixers stay healthy and Embiid feels better soon.

#2661. Notre Dame’s place in the CFP rankings is still very fluid

Notre Dame fans learned all too well last year that the college football playoff rankings are something more of an art form than science. It's funny how a body that proclaims it uses a handful of metrics eventually falls apart due to odd formatting and embedded notions about who is actually good — and made up reasons to support made up reasons.

The art is terrible, and the math never has the work actually shown.

Notre Dame is currently No. 4 with one game left for them, but two weeks of college football still left to be played. More than any other team in the rankings, Notre Dame is vulnerable because they are who they are. The Irish have a seat, a strong voice, ands a vote at the CFP table — but they are certainly outnumbered in sentiment.

But that's the preamble for disaster which is damn near impossible right now.

Still… Notre Dame could still find themselves ranked lower than No. 4 when the final rankings are released, but they could also find themselves as the No. 2 team. It's weird man, but there are still all of these games to be played, and we don't know how this will all end up. It frustrates me to no end that so many look at these brackets they publish based off of the latest set of rankings and call them a "projection." It's not a projection — it's a reflection of the current seeding of which NO ONE expects to be the same in a few weeks.

There's also the argument/debate between Notre Dame fans about what's better, a bye or a first round game?

There were several questions in the comments of the announcement post, that I want to answer.

I think if it's Wake Forest that wins the ACC championship with a 12-1 record, they will jump into the top 4.

Texas will drop one spot if they lose the SEC Championship.

Of course… Duke could beat Wake Forest and Texas A&M could beat Texas this week, and none of that matters.

The rankings are still very, very fluid and all Notre Dame can do is win on Saturday and see how this lines up. A win guarantees a place in the CFP, and that is all they were expecting last year before they were screwed out of the opportunity.

#2659. The “Julian Champagnie for Three-Point Contest” campaign begins here

Having the Spurs well represented at All-Star Weekend the last few years has been a new feeling, and I'm not just talking about the Rising Stars Challenge or the main event. Stephon Castle and Carter Bryant came in as runners up in the Dunk Contest the last two years, marking San Antonio's first representation there since the 1980's. Victor Wembanyama also participated in the Skills Challenge in both his rookie and sophomore campaigns (to not-so-great results, as Anthony Edwards' horsing around cost Team Top Pick the first time, then Wemby and Chris Paul's attempts to cheese it got them disqualified in the second go-round.)

But one event the Spurs have always felt underrepresented at is the Three-Point Contest. Despite being one of the teams that helped to revolutionize the three-pointer and often having some of the top shooters in the league, their history there is limited to Steve Smith (2002), Roger Mason (2009), Matt Bonner (2013) and Marco Belinelli (2014 winner, 2015). And Bonner basically had to plead and even campaign for himself to get in.

The Spurs have had many more deserving participants than that, but it's no lie that the league likes to go for trendier names since these events suffer enough for viewership as it is, and this is an event superstars can participate in without fear of injury or overexertion. Perhaps the most obvious gimmick ever was allowing Damian Lillard to participate last season despite not playing in a single game while recovering from a ruptured Achilles. Was he medically cleared to shoot threes? Of course. Was it a feel-good story? It was, but was it fair to perhaps another deserving participant who played the whole season and otherwise missed out on some bonus money? That is the ultimate question, and I can easily name one such player: Julian Champagnie.

Champagnie is the ultimate feel-good story himself. Undrafted out of St. Johns, he signed a two-way contract with the 76ers in 2022, just to be waived for Mac McClung, whom they only wanted to represent them at the Dunk Contest before he was waived himself. Their loss was the Spurs' gain, and they quickly grabbed him to help with their lack of shooters, and he's been filling that gap beautifully ever since.

Whether starting or coming off the bench, he has always been one of the steadier hands in the NBA. Even though he initially began last season off the bench, he kept finding himself filling in for injured starters before eventually taking over the starting power forward position for good, after Harrison Barnes fell into a slump he couldn't escape, and it became obvious that having Champangie out there either took defensive pressure off Wemby, or defenders forgot about him and left him wide open. More often than not, he made them pay by hitting 38.1% on over six attempts per game. That shooting carried over into the playoffs, where he hit 39.6% of his threes as a starter for a team that made the finals.

This year has been even more of the same in terms of being in and out of the starting lineup, except he's shooting even better. While it's still early, he's currently shooting 41.7% on 7 attempts per game, both career highs. Because the season is still young, that "only" places him at 38th in the league in three-point percentage, but amongplayers who have played in the majority of games and are shooting at least 7 attempts per game, that places him behind only Desmond Bane, Duncan Robinson, Klay Thompson, Steph Curry, Grayson Allen and Jamal Murray. That's six players, and the contest has eight participants. Odds are as the season progresses, the real shooters of the league will begin to separate themselves, and Champagnie will be one of them.

With the Spurs having all the eyes on them now, surely the league will want them well represented at All-Star Weekend. While Wemby is a shoo-in for the All-Star game itself, no one else really is, so maybe putting their best shooter in the Three-Point Contest will be a good start. If Champagnie keeps this up, he'll be more than deserving, and hopefully it won't take a Matt Bonner campaign to get it done, but in case it does, we're starting it right here.

Today is November 24, 2026, and with the zero power I have, I am officially nominating Julian Champagnie for the 2027 Three-Point Contest in the Footprint Center in Phoenix, Arizona on Feburary 20. Who's with me?

#2653. Quick strikes in first half sink Houston Dynamo in playoff-opening loss to San Jose Earthquakes

Poor set piece defending doomed the Houston Dynamo in Tuesday's playoff match versus the San Jose Earthquakes.

The Earthquakes scored two first-half goals off a corner and a free kick Tuesday to dispatch the Dynamo 2-1 in Game 1 of the Western Conference first-round series at PayPal Park in San Jose, Calif.

"In the playoffs, everybody has to be at their best and then you have to play a smart, intelligent game," Houston coach Ben Olsen said. "Those two things have to add up if you're going to win in the playoffs."

Game 2 will be at 1:30 p.m. Saturday at Shell Energy Stadium, with the Dynamo needing a victory to force a deciding Game 3 in San Jose.

San Jose captain Ronaldo Vieira opened the scoring with a short-range header in the 11th minute off a corner kick. Winger Timo Werner whipped in a cross to the front of the goal. Viera, in position to screen goalkeeper Jonathan Bond and left unmarked by any defenders, headed it into the net without impediment.

"That should never happen," Olsen said. "I don't think we've given up a near stick corner all year."

Eduard Löwen doubled the advantage with a beautiful long-range free kick 13 minutes later. He had already forced a great save out of Bond earlier in the match on a free kick but this shot, from around 32 yards out, curved and dipped to his left and out of the reach of Dynamo goalie.

Löwen's goal comes just a day after winning the MLS Comeback Player of the Year award. Lowen's wife, Ilona, died earlier in the year of Stage 4 brain cancer. Tuesday's game was the 29-year-old German's first playoff game since Ilona had been diagnosed with cancer in 2024.

"Credit to the goalkeeper on the first one, that was an amazing save," Löwen said on Apple TV after the match. "I thought I'd go the same way again, but then I thought maybe I try the other way. Thank God it worked out."

Houston's best chance in the first half came when the ball found Héctor Herrera outside the box with San Jose goalkeeper Earl Edwards Jr. off his line. But Löwen cleared Herrera's looping shot from in front of the goal.

Herrera started the match just days after being charged with driving while intoxicated last weekend in Montgomery County.

The Dynamo came out stronger in the second half but a goal remained elusive until Duncan McGuire scored in the 80th minute. Mateusz Bogusz crossed in a ball from the left wing that McGuire redirected it into the net.

It was only the second goal for McGuire since joining Houston from Orlando City SC in the summer.

"Great ball in from (Bogusz)," McGuire said. "The ball was perfect, and it came off well. I'm glad to get a goal."

But the Dynamo had no time to build any momentum off the goal before starting center back Agustin Resch got red carded for taking down Ousseni Bouda outside the Houston box after turning the ball over just a minute later.

Resch, a rookie who was sixth on the team in minutes this season, will be suspended for Saturday's Game 2 at Shell Energy Stadium.

The Dynamo need to win to force a winner-take-all Game 3 on Dec. 2 back in Northern California.

"It was a tricky week," Olsen said. "I don't want to get into all that, but it's not an excuse. But hopefully, we can all look ourselves in the mirror, get back and understand that all we have to do is win a game to get back here and try this again."

#2651. What are the worst losses for each Super Bowl-winning team?

The Minnesota Vikings are coming off a particularly tough showing in a 35-10 loss to the San Francisco 49ers in Mexico City on Sunday night. One thing I hear a lot after games like this is, "Well, you're definitely not a Super Bowl contender if you can lose a game by 25 points."

The last team to lose a game by 25-plus points and win a Super Bowl in the same season? It wasn't that long ago — the Tom Brady-led Tampa Bay Buccaneers six seasons ago lost 38-3 in Week 9 to the New Orleans Saints.

The average deficit for the 59 previous Super Bowl winners who lost a game — pop that champagne, remaining surviving 1972 Miami Dolphins — was 15.4 points.

I don't know that any of these numbers truly mean anything, but it felt too interesting not to share.

#2650. St. John's outlasts Ducks in Players Era quarterfinal

The Oregon Ducks men's basketball team looked pretty good in the first three games. But then reality set in.

After a loss to Oregon State, the Ducks went on to Las Vegas, where St. John's exposed every single weakness this team has in a 90-79 defeat in the Players' Era Championship.

As a result, Oregon gets "rewarded" by getting to play No. 5 Texas Tech on Thanksgiving.

The Ducks were down by more than 15 points for most of the second half, but Oregon was able to stage a rally to cut the deficit into single digits towards the end of the game. Unfortunately for the Ducks, St. John's figured out they were able to get the rim almost at will to cut down any rally Oregon try to stage

For the entire first half and much of the second half, St. John's press baffled Oregon all night, as the Ducks committed 15 turnovers. The Red Storm also had superior speed on both ends of the floor, which led to contested shots for Oregon and easy buckets for the Red Storm. The Ducks' lack of defensive fundamentals and footwork led to a bunch of layups for St. John's. At times, it seemed as if defense was optional for Oregon.

There was one bright spot for the Ducks with the revelation of Jerry Easter II. The transfer from USC played sparingly in the first four games, but in this contest, Easter scored 14 points to lead Oregon, 13 of those coming in the second half alone. Jasper Johnson added 13, and Fred Payne scored 12 for the Ducks.

But that was not nearly enough to counter the Red Storm's offensive attack. Ian Jackson led all scorers with 21 points. St. John's ended up with four players in double figures. Once the Red Storm figured out they could get to the rim off that will, it was fairly easy for them to score. The end of the game with 52 points in the paint.

Oregon did shoot 51 percent from the field, but finished just 20-of-29 from the free-throw line and a paltry 3-of-15 from the three-point line.

There's been a lot of talk of how the Ducks have a lot of depth, which they do, but Head Coach Tony Stubblefield is going to have to cut down that rotation to eight or nine players in order to develop some chemistry. That showed up in a big way in this game, as Oregon just had nine assists on the 28 baskets made.

John Ourand of Puck reports in his Varsity newsletter that the NFL and YouTube have been negotiating a three-game package for the 2027 season. The arrangement would include a Christmas Eve game, the Week 17 Saturday game to be televised by NBC, and the Week 10 European game that was televised by Fox.

This year, Christmas Eve lands on a Thursday; Prime Video will televise the Texans-Eagles game that night (barring a flex). Next year, Christmas Eve lands on a Friday.

YouTube was at one point negotiating the five-game package for 2026 that landed with Netflix. It includes Wednesday night's first-of-its-kind Thanksgiving Eve game between the Packers and Rams. YouTube walked, as Ourand reported at the time, when the league tried to split the five-game package between multiple partners.

The arrangement between the NFL and YouTube currently includes Sunday Ticket. That package could be disappearing in the next round of broadcast deals.

The inevitable expansion of the regular season to 18 games per team will create another 16 games that can be sliced and diced into special packages.

#2646. Michigan does about-face on Trev Alberts, potentially owing him $17.2 million

The last time Trev Alberts made this kind of a stir, he was the subject of Bill Tobin’s legendary rant against Mel Kiper.

This time, the situation potentially involves a significant payment to Alberts.

Via ESPN, Michigan backed out of an agreement to hire Alberts (who played in only 29 career games over three seasons after being the fifth overall pick in the 1994 draft) to become the university’s next athletic director. Alberts told ESPN that he had signed a “binding memorandum of understanding” for the position.

Alberts’s lawyer, Tom Mars, told ESPN that Michigan owes Alberts a $17.2 million buyout.

For that kind of money, Michigan will be very tempted to refuse to pay, forcing litigation and the expense, uncertainty, and delay that goes along with it. Alberts could decide to take less than he’s owed, simply to end the fight.

Of course, Alberts also could become determined to prove a point — if he and Mars believe Alberts has an ironclad claim to the money.

Michigan’s about-face apparently relates to deposition testimony from Alberts in a Title IX case arising from his tenure at Nebraska. Per ESPN, Alberts gave testimony on December 4, 2025, that Michigan regards as problematic.

Alberts was asked whether he believes it’s true that college coaches should never have sex with the athletes they’re coaching. The obvious answer is, “Yes.” Alberts pursued a different strategy.

“I don’t know the answer to that,” Alberts said.

“Well, I mean, you know, it just depends,” Alberts replied.

He then said the situation could be “nuanced,” due to preexisting relationships or eligibility waivers that could result in athletes being nearly the same age as young assistant coaches.

It’s an example of the gamesmanship in which some witnesses will engage when grilled by lawyers during depositions. The lawyer wanted to get an admission from Alberts that could be used broadly, and repeatedly, in the case arising from a relationship between a women’s basketball player and an assistant coach. Alberts tried to resist by clumsily splitting hairs.

Then there’s the question of whether Michigan is genuinely troubled by the testimony, or whether the school is using it as a way to justify not hiring Alberts — and not paying him.

Whatever happens between Alberts and Michigan, it’s another example of the so-called “chaos” in college sports being not the result of players doing their best in trying to get paid but schools doing their worst in allocating resources.

If Michigan’s concerns about the testimony are legitimate and not a pretext for hiring someone else, it shows that Michigan engaged in poor vetting of Alberts before signing him to a memo of understanding. If it’s a pretext, it shows that Michigan made a hasty decision and then tried to justify a change by trumping up testimony that otherwise wouldn’t have been an issue for Michigan.

Regardless, the possibility that Michigan will owe Alberts all or part of $17.2 million is another tangible example of the fact that the “chaos” comes not from players making good decisions but from schools making bad ones.

#2645. Earthquakes make successful return to MLS playoffs with victory over Houston

Before Tuesday, it had been 14 long years since the San Jose Earthquakes had given their fans the experience of thunderous, high-pressure atmosphere of playoff soccer at home - and 23 even longer years since Quakes fans bore witness to a home playoff victory, when Landon Donovan rocketed a Golden Goal past Kansas City Wizards goalie Pat Onstead in sudden-death overtime to send San Jose to the MLS Cup they would eventually capture.

So it was only right that in their first playoff match since 2020 and their first ever in PayPal Park, the Earthquakes gave the dedicated fans who ignored oncoming storms and persevered through mind-numbing I-280 traffic a 2-1 victory over the Houston Dynamos to take the first leg of the best-of-three Round 1 series.

And the Quakes didn't keep their fans in suspense, getting the long-awaited party started early.

After left midfielder Beau Leroux won a corner kick patrolling the Dynamos box, ace striker Timo Werner delivered the ball to the near post, where central midfielder and captain Ronaldo Vierra headed it in, prompting the San Jose Ultras section to whip off their shirts and as San Jose took a 1-0 lead 11 minutes into the match.

Just 13 minutes later, as the drummers in the Epicentro fan section banged louder and louder, MLS Comeback Player of the Year Eduard Löwen squared up for a free kick a few yards outside the Dynamos box and rifled the ball over the Houston defenders, ricocheting the rock off the left post to extend the San Jose lead to 2-0.

And though the stadium grew tense after the Dynamos' Duncan McGuire found the back of the net at the 80-minute mark, San Jose held on through regulation and five minutes of stoppage time to collect its first home playoff victory in PayPal Park's history, earning a standing ovation from the Quakes fans.

Game 2 of the series will be Saturday in Houston. Should Game 3 be necessary, it would be played at PayPal Park on Dec. 2.

#2644. Knicks’ lack of wing depth is rearing ugly head with recent injuries

Since the mountain of injuries single-handedly derailed the Knicks' 2024 playoff run, they've been the pinnacle of health around the NBA.

Aside from dealing with the lack of durability from Mitchell Robinson, almost no long-term injuries have hampered the Knicks' playoff aspirations. Even the more bothersome injuries, Landry Shamet's shoulder issues, Deuce McBride's core surgery, and Jalen Brunson's nagging ankles, all resolve themselves before the postseason.

Coming off a grueling championship run and attempting an exceptionally difficult repeat in an age of parity, injuries are the looming threat that could derail things before they get started.

It's no wonder, then, that the team has been playing it safe with minor ailments to Jose Alvarado and Josh Hart over the last few weeks, but two more issues have sprung up over the last few days. Jordan Clarkson is dealing with a bout of plantar fasciitis, and OG Anunoby has a calf strain.

Both of these could easily be resolved in under a week, but could both also derail both of their seasons.

Plantar fasciitis can be managed, which is likely what the team is trying to do, but more severe bouts that build up over time could leave players out for months. Calf injuries in recent years have been a dangerous precursor for Achilles tears, as seen with Kevin Durant and Tyrese Haliburton in recent years. Even if it's a mild strain, it is imperative to take it slow.

That might mean no Anunoby for a while, even if no timetable has been presented. For a coach like Mike Brown who loves to experiment in the regular season, that might not seem like too bad.

For us fans? It means seeing some… interesting lineup combinations in close games. It's one thing when they played around with Dalton Knecht and Mo Diawara against the Bucks and Bulls, but Pacôme Dadiet? Now that's something.

Landry Shamet seems to have replaced Anunoby in the starting lineup, and although his incredible shooting and great defense are providing a spark to a starting five that usually starts sluggish (Starters w/Shamet replacing Anunoby have a +29.4 net rating in 15 minutes, compared to -12.9 with the regulars), he lacks size.

This presents a problem that the Knicks knew they had, but it has further exacerbated the team's quietest shortcoming: wing depth.

In a perfect world, Diawara would've taken the next step in his development and firmly entrenched himself in the rotation, but he's been passed over for Dadiet in the last week for those bench wing minutes vacated by the injuries. Part of me thinks it's an attempt to raise the expiring French wing's trade value, but it could be something in practice prompting this opportunity.

Since Diawara signed his four-year extension in July, there's been no sign of improvement. He struggled in Summer League and has been fairly regular in any action he's had since. That's opened the door for Dadiet, who, although seems more confident from three-point range, has also been unspectacular.

It's hard to hide them in a lineup offensively given the roster construction. Sure, ideally, you have Karl-Anthony Towns or Jalen Brunson on the court at all times, but that's just one player. When one is off the court, either Tyler Kolek or Andre Drummond is on, and neither are any threat to score.

Surround that with Hart's offensive struggles, Mikal Bridges' inconsistency, and the limited games of McBride and Shamet, and you have some painful offensive stretches. When Brown gets more involved, it gets better, but teams don't want to be constantly running stuff:

The options are extremely limited, and if you try to look deeper than Diawara or Dadiet, you get two guys who shoot and don't do much else (Tyler Nickel, Knecht). That's it.

This isn't that big of a deal if Anunoby's strain is mild and he's back soon. Injuries happen, and everyone has to eventually play the end of the bench in unenviable situations over a grueling 82-game season, so Brown will just hold his nose and rely on his army of small-to-medium-sized guards in these spots and hope they won't get burned when the better teams eventually come.

But long term, could the Knicks use another warm body?

The Knicks are unable to sign a 15th player until February 13, squarely in buyout market territory, and it's far too soon to tell who could be available. There's also the trade deadline with some interesting contract situations on the roster, but is getting an insurance policy the top priority over, say, an upgrade at backup center?

We're well past the Vince Goodwill fake panic of the first few weeks, and the Knicks are sitting pretty in a three-way tie at second in the East through 17 games, but maybe the front office will need to get to work on more than they originally thought they would have to.

#2640. ‘Can’t Wait For This Coaching Staff To Be Out’ — Irritated Colts Fans Question Harsh Film Room Treatment of Anthony Richardson

The Indianapolis Colts are turning to Anthony Richardson at quarterback after waiving Daniel Jones, giving the 2023 first-round pick another opportunity to establish himself as the team's long-term option.

However, comments from offensive coordinator Jim Bob Cooter about Richardson's preparation have since prompted a wave of frustration among Colts fans, with several questioning how the coaching staff has handled the quarterback.

Richardson is preparing for his first start since the 2024 season after spending much of the current campaign behind Jones. Despite Jones struggling at times, head coach Shane Steichen stuck with him until the organization decided to make a change.

Cooter recently discussed Richardson's experience in the quarterback room, pointing out that he has had the chance to observe several players and their weekly preparation routines. The offensive coordinator suggested that seeing different approaches could give Richardson a broader understanding of how quarterbacks prepare for opposing defenses.

"We've obviously had an interesting four years at (QB). But Anthony's got to watch a lot of different guys go through their weekly process … of preparing for an opponent," Cooter said.

"It can be nice to have that 10,000-foot view," Cooter added.

The comments quickly drew criticism from Colts fans, with some questioning why the coaching staff continues to insinuate that Richardson's prep is lagging behind as he gets ready to return to the starting lineup.

One frustrated fan wrote, "Can't wait for this coaching staff to be out."

Another questioned whether the repeated references to preparation suggested Richardson had struggled with that aspect of his game. "Dude, AR must be awful at preparation for how much they harp on it," the user wrote.

With the starting job now available, Richardson has an opportunity to change the conversation around his future in Indianapolis.

Steichen has also addressed speculation about their relationship, insisting that the two remain in regular communication.

"I think we're in a really good place. I know there is a lot of stuff out there, but me and him, we still talk regularly, and I'm excited for his opportunity. He's matured over these years. He puts in good work, and now he gets another opportunity. I'm really looking forward to seeing him go out and compete on Sunday," Steichen said.

Richardson's return also gives Steichen an opportunity to test out the new dynamics in offense through the quarterback's mobility. The Colts have struggled this season, with their passing game ranking near the bottom of the league.

Malik Mustapha celebrating in an NFL game against the Vikings last Sunday. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

Seahawks wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba running with the ball during an NFL game. Getty Images

49ers defense celebrating in an NFL game against the Dallas Cowboys. AP Photo/Tony Gutierrez

#2637. Observations after Sixers' 5-game win streak ends with blowout loss to Blazers

Observations after Sixers' 5-game win streak ends with blowout loss to Blazers originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers' five-game winning streak was snapped Monday night by the Trail Blazers.

With a 128-111 defeat at Xfinity Mobile Arena, the Sixers dropped their first game of the year against Western Conference opposition and fell to 14-4. Portland improved to 11-6.

LeBron James had a season-high 23 points and six rebounds. Tyrese Maxey scored 22 points and Jaylen Brown added 20.

Deni Avdija led the Blazers with 31 points and seven assists. Donovan Clingan posted 15 points and 18 rebounds.

The Sixers were missing Joel Embiid (illness). Ja Morant (left hamstring strain) and Shaedon Sharpe (right knee meniscus surgery) were among Portland's sidelined players.

Next on the Sixers' schedule is a Wednesday night game vs. the Heat. Here are observations on their blowout loss to the Blazers:

Jabari Walker, listed at 6-foot-7, defied conventional wisdom by winning the opening tip-off against the 7-2 Cllingan. Maxey then canned a three-pointer.

Brown scored the Sixers' next four points with a pair of free throws and a short jumper. VJ Edgecombe's layup gave the team a 9-2 lead. Brown and Dean Wade both returned Monday after sitting out the last two games with left hamstring injuries.

Avdija got hot in the first quarter. He scored 11 quick points, made his first four field goals and helped the Blazers avoid a serious early deficit.

The Sixers took a 32-30 edge with 9.3 seconds left in the first when Walker jammed in a put-back dunk. The former Portland second-round draft pick played 17 minutes in his second start of the season and continued to look deserving of a rotation spot. He posted 10 points and five rebounds.

Adem Bona was available again following an eight-game absence with a cervical spine sprain. However, Dominick Barlow checked in first to back up Walker.

Barlow had an outstanding start to his night. He scored a clever lefty push shot over Clingan and threw down a dunk in the first quarter. Barlow also made a highlight defensive play in his opening stint, defending Avdija in isolation and rejecting his layup attempt.

Bona then subbed in for Barlow with 3:23 left in the first quarter. He had a positive first possession, grabbing an offensive rebound and driving in for a dunk.

Wade later played at center, too. Barlow logged 16 minutes and had six points. Bona recorded four points and two boards in five minutes. Sixers head coach Nick Nurse ended up using a 10-man rotation and did not play rookie guard Labaron Philon Jr. until fourth-quarter garbage time.

Overall, the Sixers' defense remained considerably worse without Embiid. The team also conceded 15 offensive rebounds, including five to Clingan.

"I think your rim protection and ability to do that with some size is always a focal point of being really good defensively," Nurse said. "And then you've got to do it a little bit by committee (with Embiid out). I thought, for the most part, I was looking at possessions where I liked our help into the paint. They were doing a good job of zinging it out.

"I didn't particularly like our (defense) back out. … There were a couple of times they missed those and still got rebounds. We were compacted in the lane with everybody because we didn't get back out, and then still giving up an offensive rebound as well. That's just playing through the possession, a little bit of energy, all that kind of stuff. … We just didn't do enough pieces well."

Brown delivered tons of efficient offense for the Sixers in the first half and sure didn't appear rusty. His layup late in the second quarter tied the game at 58-all. The five-time All-Star scored 19 first-half points on 8-for-10 shooting.

Avdija exceeded Brown's production, hitting heat-check threes, leaners through contact and just about everything he put up regardless of the defender. He tallied 25 points in the first half and shot 9 for 12 from the field.

James reached 16 points when he capped a high-scoring half by nailing a corner three. The contest was even at 69 apiece heading into halftime.

Monday's game was James' first of the season with three or more made three-pointers. The four-time MVP went 4 for 5 beyond the arc. He'd gone 10 for 46 (21.7 percent) over his first 13 games and was due for a good long-range night.

James was whistled for his third foul early in the third quarter. Brown picked up his fourth with 10:15 to go in the period, forcing him to sit for an extended stretch.

"I wasn't too happy about it. … I think that affected the game," Brown said. "It also affected my rhythm a little bit in the second half. I had to sit (almost) the whole third quarter. Coming back from injury, coming back from a hamstring thing, my body didn't really feel the same after that."

Brown noted postgame that he had "a little bit of soreness and stuff like that."

"I think everything will check out," he said. "The medical staff is on top of everything. Those hamstrings are tricky, so you want to make sure you play it the right way, be safe. I also don't want to miss a lot of games, so I might be out there, but I've also got to be smart. I think I played it the right way today."

Avdija stopped lighting up the Sixers in the third period, but the team still had another unimpressive defensive quarter. Portland posted 32 points in the third and built its lead to double figures in the opening minute of the fourth.

The game devolved into a blowout. An Avdija dunk put the Blazers' advantage at 22 points with 5:15 on the clock and the Sixers didn't have a miracle comeback in store.

Even with all their wins, there's no question the Sixers have been trending downward on defense over the past couple of weeks, allowing regular dribble penetration and plenty of comfortable threes.

They'll aim to raise their level on that side of the floor and expect Embiid's presence to be a major help once he's back in action.

"I think it's just mindset," Walker said. "We're capable when we want to. You need games like this every now and then just to remind you that it's not as easy as it feels sometimes. It takes effort every game.

"I think we can learn a lot from this. It's just part of the growing pains, but I'm confident we'll get back to that (early-season) level of defense. We have what it takes."

"I know what type of player I am," Adebo said. "I know what I can do on the field. I know what type of person I am, so I don't think it's anything new necessarily that I've learned about myself, but certainly just staying prepared and ready to go when you're called upon."

Only 20 months after signing a three-year, $54 million contract as the prize of the Giants' 2025 free agent class, Adebo was inactive against the Commanders because backup cornerbacks Colton Hood and Nic Jones offered more special teams value. #2631. Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double

Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers stayed unbeaten Saturday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena, earning a 127-116 win over the Bucks and improving to 3-0 on the season.

Joel Embiid had his 10th career regular-season triple-double, tallying 28 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists.

On his 30th birthday, Jaylen Brown posted 27 points and five assists. Tyrese Maxey had 26 points. VJ Edgecombe scored 17 and grabbed 13 boards.

The Sixers' absences on the first night of a back-to-back included LeBron James (low back/sciatica management). Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said pregame that he did not know yet who would be available for his team's matchup with the Pistons on Sunday.

Here are observations on the Sixers' victory Saturday:

Dean Wade made his Sixers debut and started in James' place. He'd missed the first two games of the regular season with a left ankle sprain.

The 3-and-D forward scored the night's first points by a sinking a corner three-pointer on the opening possession.

Embiid also had a sharp start. He moved well, made good decisions and served as the main hub of his team's offense in the early going.

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center has often enjoyed facing Myles Turner. He entered the night with an average of 29.4 points in 18 previous games against the Bucks big man.

Embiid did a little bit of everything in the first quarter, posting eight points, four assists and four rebounds over nine minutes. After snatching an offensive board, Embiid drained a fadeaway jumper to give the Sixers a 10-1 lead.

One of Embiid's assists was quite stylish. He found Edgecombe open beyond the arc with a behind-the-back bounce pass. Edgecombe knocked down the shot and wound up going 3 for 4 from three-point range in the first quarter.

The Sixers added rookie Labaron Philon Jr. to their rotation. Jabari Walker stayed in the mix, though he didn't enter until the 7:36 mark of the second quarter.

Philon played four minutes in his NBA debut and missed his lone shot attempt, a corner three. On defense, Philon allowed a couple of blow-bys off the dribble. He generally looked like he belonged on offense, albeit without any production in his brief run.

Maxey banked in a half-court heave at the first-quarter buzzer to put the Sixers up nine points. The Sixers couldn't carry forward any momentum, however, and began the second quarter poorly.

Adem Bona had another rough stint amid a subpar start to the season. After Anfernee Simons missed a transition layup try, Ryan Rollins' three lifted the Bucks into a 40-37 lead.

The dreadful stretch for the Sixers on both sides of the ball called to mind how they'd fallen into a 29-point deficit Thursday night vs. the Cavaliers before clawing out a comeback win.

The Sixers mustered just seven points in first six minutes of the second quarter and had many stagnant possessions that concluded with contested jumpers. The team's transition defense was dismal for much of the second period. Milwaukee had the game's first 19 fast-break points.

The Sixers regained the lead late in the second quarter. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope made two three-balls in the second and nabbed three first-half steals. Embiid assisted a go-ahead, and-one Walker layup.

Brown hit a three with 11.8 seconds left in the second quarter. Unsurprisingly, his variety of shotmaking skills were useful without James in the lineup.

Even when James or Embiid sit, the Sixers should have a simple advantage in terms of volume of stars over most opponents this year. None of Brown, Embiid or Maxey had the sort of off night that would have improved the Bucks' odds of a road win. They'd all passed the 20-point mark by the end of the third quarter.

Maxey notched another final-possession bucket, this time with a more conventional make. He canned a jumper from the right elbow with 1.7 seconds left in the third to extend the Sixers' lead to 97-87.

The Bucks made a late push in the fourth quarter. Kel'el Ware's put-back, and-one layup cut the Milwaukee's deficit to 117-114.

The Sixers ultimately handled business. Embiid reached his triple-double by assisting a second-chance Brown jumper and and Caldwell-Pope soon drilled a dagger corner three. Embiid even threw down a last-minute dunk for good measure.

For the second consecutive season, the Sixers have a 3-0 start. They got to four wins last year before dropping their first game.

#2628. Sixers' record-setting wait for the West ends against Trail Blazers

Sixers' record-setting wait for the West ends against Trail Blazers originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Have you noticed anything different about the Sixers' season?

No, not the fact that LeBron James and Jaylen Brown are wearing red, white and blue and have helped Philadelphia build an Eastern Conference-leading 14-3 record.

The difference is hidden in their schedule. All 17 games have come against Eastern Conference opponents.

When the Sixers welcome the Portland Trail Blazers to Xfinity Mobile Arena on Monday night, it will mark the latest they have ever gone into a season before facing a Western Conference team.

Philadelphia's 18-game wait also ties the 1979-80 Atlanta Hawks for the second latest by an Eastern Conference team. Only the 1980-81 Milwaukee Bucks went longer, meeting the West for the first time in their 21st game.

The Sixers have played who has been placed in front of them and won five consecutive games. They have already beaten the Knicks twice and own victories over Cleveland and Detroit.

Their first Western Conference matchup introduces a different comparison.

The West entered Monday with 11 teams above .500. The East had seven. Western Conference teams were also 41-20 against the East through Sunday.

Portland will not answer every question about how the Sixers compare with the other conference. It begins a more varied portion of their schedule.

The Sixers will face Memphis and Denver on consecutive nights next week. Dallas and Houston visit later in December before Philadelphia travels to play the Lakers, Clippers, Kings and Suns over a six-day stretch.

Portland is 10-6 under first-year head coach Micah Nori, the father of Phillies prospect Dante Nori.

The Blazers are averaging 116.1 points while allowing 110.3 per game, with both figures ranking in the top 10. Their 15.4 made three-pointers per game rank second in the NBA.

Deni Avdija leads Portland with 23.9 points per game. Damian Lillard is averaging 20.6 points in his return to the franchise, while 7-foot-2 center Donovan Clingan has supplied size around a deep group of guards and wings.

Clingan posted 22 points and 13 rebounds Saturday night at Madison Square Garden. Portland erased a 26-point deficit and briefly took the lead before Mikal Bridges made a game-winning three-pointer at the buzzer.

The 97-96 loss dropped the Blazers to 1-3 over their last four games. Slow starts have followed them during that stretch.

"Our last three games, we haven't gotten off to great starts, and that's just something that we got to correct," Lillard said. "Our energy and our focus and our intent has to be better from the jump. We can't let this trend continue."

The Sixers know something about overcoming early deficits. Six of their 14 victories have required double-digit comebacks.

Portland will be missing two major pieces. Ja Morant is out with a left hamstring strain, while Shaedon Sharpe remains sidelined following right meniscus surgery.

Even without Morant, the Blazers can turn to Lillard, Jrue Holiday and Scoot Henderson to initiate their offense. Avdija and Toumani Camara provide size on the perimeter, while Clingan gives Portland the kind of interior presence that has occasionally troubled the Sixers.

Anfernee Simons and Jabari Walker know the Portland organization better than any other Sixers.

The two shared the floor for 128 games with the Trail Blazers. Portland won 43 of them.

Their responsibilities have changed in Philadelphia. So have the expectations.

Simons scored 18 points in each of the Sixers' last two games and made seven three-pointers. He started in place of Tyrese Maxey against Orlando and hit the clinching three in his hometown. Three nights later, he supplied four more threes off the bench in the Sixers' 132-129 win over Milwaukee.

Walker has also found steady work during the Sixers' recent frontcourt injuries. He recorded nine points, seven rebounds and four assists against the Bucks after scoring 11 against Indiana and hitting a go-ahead three late in Orlando.

Both players recently discussed how their difficult seasons in Portland changed their perspective on filling smaller roles for a winning team.

"You feel appreciative of the times where you go into a situation where your role might be a little bit less, but you're winning," Simons said. "That's something that you can't take for granted, for sure, because it's hard to win in the NBA. We've seen it firsthand."

Their former team will now see them operating within a deeper rotation than the one Philadelphia carried through much of the past week.

Brown, Dean Wade and Adem Bona were all listed as probable on the Sixers' initial injury report after missing time.

Brown and Wade have each missed the last two games. Bona has been sidelined since Nov. 4 because of a cervical spine sprain. Dominick Barlow returned Saturday and scored 12 points on 5-for-6 shooting in his season debut.

Joel Embiid was added to the injury report Monday morning as questionable because of an illness. His availability will determine how the Sixers approach Clingan and Robert Williams III inside.

The Sixers have leaned on smaller lineups and reserve contributors while Nurse has managed injuries across the roster. Monday could give him more options, even if Embiid cannot play.

FanDuel Sportsbook listed the Sixers as 3.5-point favorites Monday afternoon. Philadelphia was -152 on the moneyline, Portland was +128 and the over-under was 229.5.

The Blazers are 7-4 on the road. The Sixers are 7-2 at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

After 17 games within their own conference, the Sixers will finally see what their early success looks like against the other side.

#2625. LeBron Log No. 6: A Rocky night, a shooting lesson and a fight over ‘Bron'

LeBron Log No. 6: A Rocky night, a shooting lesson and a fight over 'Bron' originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

It was another eventful week for LeBron James.

That's why we started the LeBron Log in the first place.

The King spent his latest week taking his teammates to the movies, fighting over his name in federal court and producing his best three-point shooting performance as a Sixer days after recording a podcast about the craft.

This week also marks 20 years since James faced the Sixers alongside Allen Iverson.

James found an appropriate choice for the Sixers' latest team outing.

He organized a private screening of I Play Rocky on Friday night for players, their families and members of the basketball operations staff. The film follows Sylvester Stallone's fight to get the original Rocky made while insisting that he play the title character.

"I mean, it's Rocky. We in Philly," James said. "I heard it was a great movie, and we had a night off. I've got a few connections, and I was able to bring that to my teammates and this organization for us to watch it. I thought it was a great movie. Unbelievably cast. Everyone looked like exactly who they were portraying. That is Hollywood for you. It was pretty cool."

The Sixers shared photos of James alongside Jaylen Brown, Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, Labaron Philon Jr., Jabari Walker, Tacko Fall and Adem Bona.

"Movie night, courtesy of LeBron," the team wrote.

The nationwide release of I Play Rocky came less than two weeks before Philadelphia celebrates the 50th anniversary of the original film on Dec. 3.

Nick Nurse could not attend because of a previous commitment, but he received positive reviews from his players.

"They went, they said it was very good, they loved it," Nurse said. "The big takeaway was how much Anthony actually looked like Rocky. Or Sylvester Stallone. One in the same."

James' first season in Philadelphia now includes a private Rocky screening. A trip up the Art Museum steps remains available for a future edition.

James and Steve Nash devoted the latest episode of their Mind the Game podcast to the art of shooting.

The two examined shooting form, confidence, repetitions, free throws and some of their favorite jumpers. James also revealed one detail that can affect what he does after catching the ball.

"I'm a guy who don't like shooting against the laces," James said. "So sometimes I'll come up on a quick stop and I'm about to raise and I can feel the laces not fixed. I'll turn that into a pump fake."

The episode was released Nov. 17, while James was experiencing an extended struggle from three-point range. It did not provide an instant fix.

James went 1 for 5 from three against Orlando and missed his lone attempt against Milwaukee. He entered Monday night's meeting with Portland shooting 21.7 percent from deep through his first 13 games.

James made all three of his first-half attempts from three. He ended the second quarter by pump-faking, stepping to his left and beating the buzzer with a corner three that tied the game at 69.

Nobody could see where the laces sat on the catch. The pump fake was clear.

James finished 4 for 5 from three and scored a season-high 23 points on 8-for-13 shooting. It was his third consecutive game with at least 20 points, following 22 against Orlando and 21 against Milwaukee.

The Sixers lost to Portland, 128-111, but James produced his best long-range performance since joining them.

Six days after discussing the art of shooting, he provided a brief demonstration.

James is also attempting to protect one of his most recognizable nicknames.

James and LBJ Trademarks LLC filed a federal lawsuit on Nov. 17 against PlayVision Inc. and its founders over a sports-betting research app initially called "Bron."

The complaint alleges that the company used an AI-generated version of James in an advertisement without his permission. The figure wore a No. 23 jersey with "Bron" across the back and resembled James through its voice, build and tattoos.

It also scrolled through wagers involving NBA players.

The lawsuit alleges that the advertisement falsely created the impression that James endorsed the app and suggested that he considered betting on NBA games. The complaint said the video received roughly 1 million views before it was removed.

"The integrity of NBA competition, and the public's confidence that players are not betting on the games they play, is of paramount importance to the league, its players and its fans," the complaint said. "Any suggestion that an active NBA player is betting on NBA games is therefore far from a trivial matter, and it should not be used for clicks and views."

The app offered odds comparisons, betting trends and tracking tools but did not directly accept wagers, according to its developer.

PlayVision renamed it "Evie" on Nov. 18, one day after James filed the lawsuit. James is seeking an injunction and unspecified damages. The case remains active in the Southern District of New York.

CLEVELAND – NOVEMBER 25: LeBron James #23 of the Cleveland Cavaliers looks to pass off when double teamed by the Philadelphia 76ers November 25, 2006 at The Quicken Loans Arena in Cleveland, Ohio. Copyright 2006 NBAE (Photo by David Liam Kyle/NBAE via Getty Images)

James spent Thanksgiving weekend in 2006 on the other side of the Sixers-Cavaliers matchup.

On Nov. 25, 2006, a 21-year-old James recorded 25 points, 11 assists, four rebounds and one block in Cleveland's 108-95 win over Philadelphia.

Donning the Cavs' old-school orange threads, he played nearly 41 minutes.

Iverson led the Sixers with 31 points. Andre Iguodala added 17 points and eight rebounds, while Kyle Korver made three three-pointers off the bench.

James recorded 11 assists that night. Nearly 20 years later, another 11-assist performance against Indiana moved him past Jason Kidd for third place in NBA history.

The 2006 meeting also came near the end of Iverson's original run with Philadelphia. The Sixers traded him to Denver less than a month later.

James was 21. Iverson was nearing his departure.

Twenty years later, James is wearing a Sixers uniform and Iverson's No. 3 hangs above his home floor.

Rasmus Hojlund enjoyed a dream return to Manchester on Tuesday night, finding the net for Napoli in a thrilling Champions League encounter at the Etihad Stadium. Hojlund could not resist taking a swipe at his former cross-town rivals during Tuesday's 2-2 draw in the Champions League. After firing the Italian side into an early lead, the former United man was spotted mouthing a provocative message toward the City faithful, who had spent the opening stages of the match jeering his every touch. "The celebration after the goal? I was very happy with my goal. The [City] fans were booing me, so I told them there's only one club in Manchester," Hojlund explained with a grin when speaking to Sky Sport Italia.

Their only victory in the competition so far was a high-scoring 4-3 win over Bodo/Glimt.

Hojlund remains optimistic that the Partenopei can turn their fortunes around as the season progresses. "We were really happy with the game and the result. It was a difficult season for us so far, but there's a long way to go, so we can turn things around. We've got to stay positive, listen to the coach, and keep working hard. We had a lot of injuries, but Napoli are coming back and we hope to get back on track in Serie A and the Champions League," the striker added.

The forward has faced criticism regarding his consistency since moving to Italy, often finding it difficult to replicate his prolific international scoring rate at club level. However, much of this has been attributed to a lack of tactical alternatives in the squad, forcing him to play almost every minute. Hojlund himself feels that luck has not always been on his side during his recent outings in a Napoli shirt.

Reflecting on his recent performances, he explained: "I think I've been quite unlucky, a couple of chances where I could've done better, but also some with good goalkeeping from the opponents. For example, the Lazio goalkeeper made some incredible saves, I also remember against Venezia it was cleared off the line."

By continuing to find the net against top-tier opposition like City, he is slowly answering the doubters who questioned his transfer fee and output. As Napoli look to climb both the Serie A table and the European standings, the fitness and form of their primary striker will be paramount. With the injury crisis slowly abating, the Danish star believes the team is ready to surge back into contention for major honors.

"I want to keep positive, I scored lots of goals on international duty, I scored at San Siro, against Como, against City, so I need to keep improving, listen to my teammates and coach, and hope to score more goals," Hojlund concluded.

The Detroit Lions announced on Tuesday night that former team owner Martha Firestone Ford has passed away at age 101. According to the team, she passed away at her home surrounded by family.

Ford took over as principal owner of the franchise in 2014, following the death of her husband, William Clay Ford. She held onto the role until 2020, when she bequeathed primary ownership to her daughter and current Lions owner Sheila Hamp.

Since then, Ford has been serving as Owner/Chair Emeritus of the team. Here's how the team described her role over the past six years.

In her most recent role as Owner/Chair Emeritus, Mrs. Ford supported her four children – Principal Owner/Chair Sheila Ford Hamp, Owner/Vice Chair Martha Ford Morse, Owner/Vice Chair William Clay Ford Jr., and Owner/Vice Chair Elizabeth Ford Kontulis – as they assumed leadership responsibilities within the family franchise. Today the Ford family proudly carries forward the legacy established by Mr. and Mrs. Ford, preserving the values, love, and passion that have shaped a family tradition spanning multiple generations.

During Mrs. Ford's brief stint as primary owner, the Lions made the playoffs twice (2014, 2016) and produced three winning seasons.

The team offered this official statement on Ford's passing:

"It is with heavy hearts that we acknowledge the passing of Martha Firestone Ford. Mrs. Ford inspired us all as a pillar of the Detroit community and the passionate matriarch of the Detroit Lions football team.

"She will always be remembered for her fierce loyalty to her family, her community, and the city of Detroit.

"Her presence on our sideline, in our building, and in our community will be greatly missed. We wish the entire Ford and Firestone families peace in this time of mourning."

#2609. Broncos face quick pivot to preparing for Mason Rudolph on Friday

The Black Friday game between the Broncos and Steelers was preceded by the Black Tuesday benching of quarterback Aaron Rodgers. Now, the Broncos will have to quickly pivot in their preparations.

As one source put it, the Broncos aren’t sure whether the unexpected move is a good thing or a bad thing.

Quarterbacks on winning teams don’t get benched very often. In 2004, the Giants sat Hall of Famer Kurt Warner despite a 5-4 record. But the goal then was to get rookie Eli Manning on the field. For the Steelers, they’ve made the decision that Rudolph, a veteran backup 19 regular-season starts in eight years, gives them a better chance to win.

The element of surprise could be a factor in the timing, too. It’s possible that the Steelers considered not saying anything at all.

This story is just getting started. Rodgers will surely have a reaction. And it surely won’t be a shrug of the shoulders and an acceptance that he won’t even be in uniform for the game.

Our guess? He’ll never be in a Steelers uniform again.

#2604. Nets searching for answers as early defensive collapses fuel losing streak

MINNEAPOLIS — The Nets will drag the NBA's longest losing skid into Milwaukee on Wednesday, a five-game slump, and pretty much all five losses have looked the same.

Embarrass themselves defensively in the first half. Give themselves no chance to win in the second. Scratch their heads looking for answers in the postgame.

Head coach Jordi Fernandez argues a call during the Nets' loss to the Magic in an NBA Cup game on Nov. 20, 2026 at Barclays Center. Getty Images

"That's happened already too many times, where we allow teams [to get on a roll early]. It's the best players in the world. If you allow one to go in and then everybody gets loose and makes shots, then it's a long night," Jordi Fernández said.

When asked what the biggest problem with their defense was, Julius Randle couldn't even pinpoint one.

"We've got a lot. We were better earlier in the year and now we've got slippage in multiple areas. So we've gotta figure out where it is. But defense just starts with competitive nature first and then go from there," Randle said. "It's disappointing. But all you can do is focus on where you're at and figure out how to get better. Figure out what's the problem, how we can consistently compete at a high level."

The problem is, in this skid the Nets have barely competed at any level.

CHECK OUT THE LATEST NBA STANDINGS AND NETS STATS

They've allowed more than 70 points in the first half of four of the five losses, tied with Charlotte for the league's longest slump. They've shown a concerning glass jaw, getting hit early and not hitting back.

"Defensively, we just can't give up 140 points. We let [Minnesota] catch their rhythm early, and that's what happens when you give good teams rhythm early on in the game," Mikel Brown Jr. told The Post. "We've got to cut that water off early, take away those wide-open shots."

In this five-game malaise, the Nets have allowed an average of 72.2 points and a 147.3 defensive rating in their first halves. They've conceded 55.9 percent shooting and 52.3 percent from deep and a minus-15.0 net rating.

Every single one of those stats is not only dead last in the league, but the worst by a margin.

That kind of porous defense in the first half makes the second half all but moot.

"Yes, it's always been for us to get off to a good start," Brown told The Post. "I really just feel like just disrupting them early on. Anytime we disrupt the team early on in the game, we come out and we fight hard. And sometimes we pull out the win, and sometimes we don't.

"But it's really just the early [part] in the game. You just can't let good players get great shots early on in the games. You give those looks to those great players, they're gonna start flowing, and then next thing you know, they shoot 50 percent, 55 percent from the field as a team. It's a snowball effect that we just can't have."
