#2528. What's next for the Twins? Three things Minnesota must do to make a postseason push in 2027 season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

It has been a surprisingly productive week for the Minnesota Twins. First, catcher Ryan Jeffers accepted the $23.15 million qualifying offer on Tuesday. Jeffers turned down a multi-year offer from the Twins, according to The Athletic, so he's betting on himself. Betting that he'll at least maintain his free agent stock and get paid next offseason.

Then, on Wednesday, the Twins brought back veteran righty Sonny Gray with a two-year contract worth $55 million. There's an opt-out after the first year. Gray, 37, finished fifth in the AL Cy Young voting this season and pitched wonderfully for the Twins in 2022 and 2023. He joins a rotation that, on paper, looks like one of the better starting units in the American League.

Here is Minnesota's rotation depth chart:

"I really don't take it lightly that he chose us," GM Jeremy Zoll told the Associated Press about Gray's return. "He had an abundance of options, and given where he's at in his career, I know how important it is to him. He expressed it quite directly how important it is to win, and this isn't just about having a good season or a winning season. It's about winning and going deep in the playoffs and making a real playoff run."

Matthews could land in the bullpen next season and that might be his long-term home. His stuff should be well suited to a relief role. Gray makes the rotation better and potentially the bullpen better as well by bumping Matthews to relief. Jeffers accepting the qualifying offer keeps a key middle-of-the-order bat in place. A good week for the Twins, this has been.

After a disappointing 77-85 finish this year, Minnesota has already improved significantly in the early days of the offseason. They play in the AL Central. With all due respect, it is not the most imposing division. There's no reason the Twins can't be in the division and wild card races next season. Here now is what's left on Minnesota's offseason to-do list.

Teams had until 5 p.m. ET Friday to offer their pre-arbitration and arbitration-eligible players contracts for 2027. They didn't have to sign them Friday, but they had to tender an offer; otherwise, the player immediately became a free agent. Dozens of players were cut loose at the non-tender deadline, as usual, and two players stood out as non-tender candidates for the Twins: Trevor Larnach and Royce Lewis. Larnach was indeed non-tendered, while Lewis was dealt to the Dodgers.

It's not often a player gets non-tendered after posting a .352 on-base percentage and 120 OPS+, but the writing was on the wall. The Twins had an agreement in place to trade Larnach at the deadline (Astros owner Jim Crane nixed the deal) and they have a very crowded outfield. Also, Larnach had wrist surgery earlier this month. That created some questions going into next season, and the Twins opted to cut him loose.

Larnach had one more year of control remaining and was expected to make over $6 million through arbitration in 2027. I reckon the Twins tried again to trade him prior to Friday's non-tender deadline. In the end, he was non-tendered rather than risk tying $6 million or so up in yet another outfielder, particularly one who is coming off wrist surgery.

Things got so bad this summer that Lewis, who has a .288 on-base percentage in over 1,200 plate appearances the last three years, was sent to Triple-A for a spell, and also moved across the diamond from third base to first base. The Twins could not count on him to provide offense and now he's playing a position with a high offensive bar. That made him expendable.

Lewis, 27, was under team control through 2028 and that extra year was an important consideration for the club. His salary would have been in the $5 million range next season through arbitration, which is pricey but not exorbitant. Now, Lewis will receive a fresh start with the Dodgers, where he can be one of the guys, not the former No. 1 overall pick and expected face of the franchise.

The Twins presumably did not want to give up on a player with as much talent as Lewis. At the same time, they kept trying, and it never worked.

The Twins got a head start on their offseason bullpen shopping when they acquired Jeff Hoffman at the trade deadline. He has one more year remaining on the contract and will be in the team's late-inning mix in 2027.

Here is manager Derek Shelton's bullpen unit at the moment:

Morris is not yet a household name, but he has a great arm and was dominant at times in 2026. The Twins have themselves a nice little late-inning trio in Gómez, Hoffman, and Morris. A spare starter like Matthews or Prielipp could wind up in the bullpen as well. Given the quality of their stuff, they have a chance to make a real impact as relievers.

Clearly though, the middle relief could use some help, and the Twins wouldn't need to spend big dollars to improve it. A second-tier free agent like, say, Andrew Kittredge would be a solid pickup. It's worth giving the Miami Marlins a call to see what it would take to get Anthony Bender and/or Michael Petersen. Point is, the bullpen can be improved, for sure.

The Twins have way more outfielders than outfield spots and that is in no way a bad thing. First and foremost, it allows them to use Byron Buxton as the full-time DH, which could help keep him on the field. Secondly, there's no such thing as too many good players. Depth is important and the Twins certainly have plenty of it in the outfield.

More outfielders than outfield spots is not a problem. It's just something the Twins have to figure out. Even if we assume Buxton will DH and is not part of the outfield mix, here are the outfielders Minnesota must sort through:

Rodriguez is one of the game's 50 or so best prospects and he is out of minor league options, meaning he must go through waivers to go to Triple-A. Obviously, the Twins won't waive him. Non-tendering Larnach allows the Twins to play Rodriguez alongside Jenkins and Keaschall in the outfield, keep Kreidler and Martin on the bench, and keep the others in Triple-A.

#2525. Jayson Tatum takes the blame for costly technical in Celtics' loss to Nuggets: 'I wasn't mad'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Boston Celtics coach Joe Mazzulla called on star forward Jayson Tatum to be "better" after he was called for a controversial technical foul in the closing seconds of Wednesday's 105-101 loss, which effectively sealed the game for the Denver Nuggets.

"We can't put ourselves in that position to even give the refs an opportunity to interpret it a certain type of way," Mazzulla said after the game. "Gotta be better."

With 6.4 seconds remaining, Jamal Murray worked off a huge screen from Nikola Jokić, created space with a nasty step-back on Neemias Queta and buried a difficult jumper to give the Nuggets a three-point lead. The Celtics, who had led by as many as 17 late in the first half, still had a chance to tie, however. At least, they did, until Tatum threw the ball toward referee John Goble.

The baseline official, Eric Dalen, immediately hit Tatum with a technical foul. Murray stepped to the line and made the free throw to put the Nuggets up by four.

"I told [Dalen], like, I wasn't mad. Wasn't a foul on me; we just called a timeout," Tatum said. "John Goble called a timeout and pointed at our bench. Thought he was looking this way, but yeah, he called a tech. For me, just find the female ref that was there, or the other ref, and whoever was probably closest, I should have just gave them the ball."

Jamal Murray hits a clutch jumper to extend the Nuggets the lead to 3, with 6.4 seconds remaining in regulation.The Celtics call a timeout, and Jayson Tatum throws the ball towards the ref John Goble, who wasn't looking, and receives a technical foul, which Murray converts to… pic.twitter.com/PZtzl0zs3D

Tatum's controversial technical capped a brutal second half for the Celtics and their star.

After scoring 20 points in the first half to help the Celtics build a 17-point lead, Tatum managed just four points in the second half on 2-of-6 shooting with five turnovers. Notably, he missed mid-range attempts on back-to-back possessions in the final two minutes. The first could have pushed the Celtics' lead back up to three, while the latter would have put them in front.

"The four turnovers I had in the third quarter really put us out of sync," Tatum said. "In those situations, I gotta communicate better, I gotta execute better, I gotta take care of the ball. I think that kinda put us in a hole, and was the turning point for the game."

This defeat was the first time all season that the Celtics have lost back-to-back games. Now 11-4, the Celtics are 1 ½ games back of the Philadelphia 76ers for the No. 1 seed in the Eastern Conference. Come April, when seeding battles are heating up, the Celtics may rue this one.

In the second half, as their lead melted away, the Celtics turned the ball over 11 times, were called for 20 fouls (which led to 22 Nuggets free throws) and shot 2 of 19 from 3-point range. Two of the Celtics' four defeats this season have now involved a major blown lead: 22 points against the Detroit Pistons on opening day and 17 points against the Nuggets.

Everyone on the internet loves to overreact, and that's especially true when we're talking about the NFL. Zach Pereles looked at several things that happened during Week 11, so decide for yourself whether we're all overreacting.

Statement: Jesse Minter will be one-and-done in Baltimore.Overreaction or reality: Overreaction. Lots of the Ravens' issues are out of first-year coach Jesse Minter's control. The Lamar Jackson injuries, obviously, threw the season way off course. Even Sunday's game was another example of the things Minter can't control going wrong. Justice Hill fumbled 1 yard from the end zone. LaJohntay Wester muffed two punts, one of which the Panthers recovered. Derrick Henry also lost a fumble. It's been a season from hell. But there are plenty of issues Minter has been responsible for — or at least hasn't fixed — this year. Regarded as a defensive whiz after two years as the Chargers' defensive coordinator, he now oversees a defense that ranks in the bottom half of the league in yards per game and yards per play, and in the bottom 10 in yards per pass attempt and takeaways. Simply put, it's been underwhelming at best for a team expected to contend for a championship. But the Ravens won't fire Minter at season's end. There are big-picture questions about Jackson and the entire roster, but Minter should get an offseason to tweak and improve his defense and fit it better to his defenders.

Statement: The Buccaneers have a serious Baker Mayfield problem.Overreaction or reality: Reality. The Buccaneers extended Mayfield with a three-year, $165 million deal just before the season began, after it seemed like an extension wouldn't happen. Tampa Bay must be wishing it hadn't made the deal. Mayfield is constantly banged up - he's dealing with plantar fasciitis in addition to the thumb injury that caused him to miss several games already this year - and he can't physically make his play style work. How the Buccaneers overcome this is TBD, because there are no realistic easy answers.

Statement: Jahmyr Gibbs will win Offensive Player of the Year.  Overreaction or reality: Reality. It wasn't always pretty, but Jahmyr Gibbs ground out 118 yards from scrimmage and two touchdowns in the Lions' 31-21 win over the Buccaneers. He's up to 1,502 yards from scrimmage this season and on pace to finish with 2,553. That would break Chris Johnson's all-time record of 2,509 from 2009. That, one would think, would clinch an Offensive Player of the Year award for Gibbs. Even if he doesn't break the record, Gibbs would be a deserving winner, so long as he keeps producing. He's had at least 110 yards from scrimmage in all but two games.

#2523. Royce Lewis trade grades: Dodgers land former No. 1 pick; Twins get another arm, arrow-up prospect

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Los Angeles Dodgers have added a former No. 1 overall pick. The Dodgers are set to acquire infielder Royce Lewis from the Minnesota Twins for right-hander Bobby Miller and minor-league catcher Francisco Espinoza, reports the New York Post. Neither team has announced the trade.

Lewis, 27, was a candidate to be non-tendered prior to Friday's deadline. Rather than cut him loose, the Twins were able to find a trade partner and receive something in return. The No. 1 pick in the 2017 draft has battled injuries throughout his career and posted a .288 on-base percentage the last three years. Lewis simply failed to launch with Minnesota.

The Dodgers figure to use Lewis as a platoon partner for Max Muncy at third base and could also move him around the infield as a utility guy. The Twins moved him from third base to first base this past season. Lewis has played every infield position in the big leagues, though he's had only one inning at shortstop since 2022.

Miller, 27, has been unable to build on his dynamic 2022 rookie season, when he threw 124 ⅓ innings with a 3.76 ERA. He has battled injuries and control issues since then, and the Dodgers moved him into the bullpen this past season. Miller has a 7.75 ERA in 134 ⅔ Triple-A innings the last three years and can be optioned down in 2027.

Espinoza, 19, reached Low Class-A in 2026 and hit .317/.411/.422 with three home runs and strong contact rates in 46 games. He does not rank among the top 30 Dodgers prospects at Baseball America or MLB Pipeline, but Espinoza is an arrow-up prospect and a solid return for a non-tender candidate.

Here now are our grades for the two-for-one trade.

At worst, Lewis will be a high-priced utility guy next season. He's projected to make $5 million or so through arbitration and that simply is not much for the Dodgers, who have a history of getting underperforming hitters to the next level (like Muncy). At best, Lewis could be the new Chris Taylor and reach his offensive ceiling while bouncing between positions.

Espinoza is a good prospect, not a great prospect, and Miller is a reclamation project. Those are easy players for the Dodgers to surrender to take a chance on Lewis and his upside. It may not work. Lewis could continue to get hurt and not hit, but it was a low-cost move and the chance of a reward is significant.

It's a very nice upside play for a team that has hit on a lot of upside plays over the year.

It's a bummer things didn't work out for Lewis and the Twins, but the reality is he was a non-tender candidate, and it wasn't a secret. Minnesota was able to get back a solid prospect in Espinoza and a lottery ticket arm in Miller despite having little leverage. Getting two players for Lewis is a very good outcome under the circumstances.

Giving each team an "A" suggests a win-win, and maybe it will be. There's a chance it's a lose-lose, though. Lewis may not hit, Miller may never rediscover his 2022 form, and Espinoza may not pan out. I see the vision for both teams, though and like it.

The Dodgers rolled the dice on a talented player and the Twins were able to fetch two players for someone they might have otherwise cut loose and sent into free agency.

#2522. Vanessa Bryant, widow of Kobe, denies teaming up with Pau Gasol to bid on WNBA's Sparks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Vanessa Bryant, the widow of Los Angeles Lakers legend Kobe Bryant, has denied a report that she is teaming up with two-time Lakers champion Pau Gasol to attempt to purchase the Los Angeles Sparks.

"Another rumor out today… I have never had any conversations about being an NBA or WNBA owner. If that was true I would announce it. I'm just over here undecided on what seasonal coffee flavor I like and over caffeinated," Bryant wrote on Instagram. "I can only speak for myself. I don't know what anyone else does or does not have going on."

Sports Business Journal reported on Wednesday that Bryant and Gasol were interested in the Sparks, which were put up for sale in October. Owner Mark Walter, who has been shedding assets amid an FBI and SEC investigation into his wealth management firm, is seeking a record-shattering $700 million for the franchise and its yet-unopened practice facility, according to Bloomberg. The current record for a WNBA team sale is $300 million, which Tilman Fertitta paid for the Connecticut Sun before moving the franchise to Houston to revive the Comets.

Notably, Josh Kushner and Bob Iger, who purchased the Lakers from Walter earlier this year, are reportedly uninterested in the Sparks. Los Angeles Clippers owner Steve Ballmer reportedly considered bidding on the team in 2024, but is currently prohibited for submitting a bid because he is serving a one-year suspension from the NBA over his role in the Aspiration scandal. However, at least one of the groups bidding for the Sparks, a group of investors put together by Swish Partners, would consider moving the team to Ballmer's Intuit Dome.

Gasol already has a financial stake in the WNBA, as he invested in the league's 2022 capital raise. Bryant frequently attends Sparks games and has brought WNBA players in to host clinics at the Mamba & Mambacita Sports Foundation. The late Kobe Bryant was a prominent figure in the women's basketball community, especially coaching his late daughter Gianna's AAU team. Gianna hoped to play for the University of Connecticut and presumably the WNBA afterward before tragically dying in the helicopter accident that killed her father and seven others in 2020.

Several former NBA players own or have owned minority stakes in WNBA teams, including Magic Johnson (Sparks), Dwyane Wade (Chicago Sky), Kyle Lowry (Toronto Tempo) and Grant Hill and Chris Webber (the upcoming Detroit expansion team set to begin play in 2029). However, no former NBA player holds the governorship of a WNBA team. Gasol could change that. If we expand to immediate family, Bryant could become the first spouse of a former NBA player to hold a controlling interest in a WNBA team, though at this stage, the exact structure of a possible Bryant-Gasol bid and the other investors who could be involved are not clear.

#2520. Brandon Aiyuk released: Former 49ers WR looks to resume career after years away

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Brandon Aiyuk's time in San Francisco has apparently come to an end. The 49ers have released Aiyuk, who will now look to continue his career with a new team, according to a report from ESPN.

The 49ers were given a two-week roster exemption when the NFL reinstated Aiyuk on Nov. 9. With that exemption ending on Nov. 23, the 49ers elected to move on from Aiyuk, who hasn't played an NFL game since tearing his ACL and MCL during the 2024 season. Aiyuk had signed a four-year, $120 deal with the 49ers that offseason following a tumultuous negotiation. That contract, as currently structured, still has two years remaining, with a 2027 cap hit of $40.5 million according to Over the Cap, meaning Aiyuk will likely need to clear waivers before any team formally signs him.

Aiyuk started the 2025 season on the PUP list. That November, it was reported that the 49ers voided the guaranteed money in his contract for 2026 due to lack of participation. In December, the 49ers placed him on their reserve/left squad list.

This summer, the 49ers placed Aiyuk on the reserve/did not report list (meaning the 49ers were not obligated to pay him and he did not count against their roster) after he did not report to training camp. Aiyuk had since applied for reinstatement with the NFL and was granted it earlier this month.

Before 2024, Aiyuk enjoyed a productive career with the 49ers, who selected him with the 25th overall pick in the 2020 draft. In 2022, he eclipsed 1,000 receiving yards for the first time and caught a career-high eight touchdowns. The following season, he recorded a career-high 1,342 receiving yards while helping the 49ers reach the Super Bowl.

While his recent actions in San Francisco might scare some teams off, Aiyuk will likely draw interest from teams that need help at receiver. Aiyuk has long been linked to the Commanders; he and Washington quarterback Jayden Daniels were teammates at Arizona State. The Steelers are another team that could potentially be a landing spot for Aiyuk.

Despite not having Aiyuk, the 49ers are 9-1 and would be the No. 1 seed in the NFL if the playoffs started today.

#2519. MLB rumors: Yankees moves heating up, plus latest on Tarik Skubal, Mets, Padres, Red Sox, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The uncertain 2026-27 Major League Baseball offseason is fully underway. The ongoing CBA negotiations and the near-certainty of an owner-implemented lockout on Dec. 2 loom over all, and it may indeed mean a flurry of trades and free-agent signings leading up to that date. That was certainly the case leading up to the last lockout of 2021-22, and this time around we've already seen some leading examples.

Thanks to that prospect of a hastened pace, offseason rumors are flowing. Speaking of which, we'll be here each day to round up what's out there. You can find Friday's supply just below.

The buzz at the GM Meetings last week was that the Mets offered top free agent Tarik Skubal a nine-year contract worth almost $400 million, reports MLB Network Radio. If the deal is worth at least $390 million, it would set new records for total guarantee and average annual value given to a pitcher. Here are the current pitcher contract records:

Given the player and the deep-pocketed teams involved in the bidding (Blue Jays, Dodgers, Mets, etc.), Skubal is well-positioned to shatter Yamamoto's record. He could beat Scherzer's and Verlander's record as well. The expected lockout will begin after the collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1. Skubal is likely to sign before then.

The Diamondbacks are set to acquire righty Johan Oviedo from the Red Sox for minor-league lefty Luke Dotson and a player to be named later, reports the Arizona Republic. Boston had four pitchers for the No. 5 starter's spot (Oviedo, Brayan Bello, Kutter Crawford, Tanner Houck) and always seemed likely to trade one to ease the logjam.

Acquired from the Pirates last offseason, Oviedo made just one ineffective appearance around elbow trouble in 2026. He returned from Tommy John surgery in 2025 and looked excellent, and Arizona will hope Oviedo rediscovers that magic as he gets further away from his injuries. Dotson is not a top prospect. It's a low-cost flier for the D-backs.

The Tigers have signed right-hander Troy Melton to a six-year extension worth $46.5 million, reports ESPN. There is a club option for a seventh year and escalators can push the total guarantee to $80 million. Melton still had five years of team control. The new extension buys out his five team control years and one free agent year with an option for another free agent year.

Melton, 26 next month, missed the start of the season with elbow inflammation and finished the season on the injured list with more elbow woes. Between injuries, he made 20 starts with a sub-3.00 ERA with strong under-the-hood numbers. The Tigers know him better than anyone and are obviously comfortable with Melton's medicals to lock him up long-term.

The New York Yankees have agreed to a two-year contract with veteran right-hander Jonathan Loáisiga, ESPN reports. The deal also includes a club option for 2029 and is worth roughly $18 million, according to MLB.com.

Loáisiga, 32, is coming off that strong season above for the Arizona Diamondbacks, and for his career boasts an ERA+ of 128 across parts of nine MLB seasons. He's worked in relief for almost all of that span, and eight of those nine seasons came with the Yankees.

New York Yankees general manager Brian Cashman was recently asked if he'd be willing to play Spencer Jones in center field. In response, he told media, including SNY, this:

"I would be comfortable with that. At the same time Jasson Domínguez is pounding the ball in winter ball. The entire industry is noticing that based on the phone calls I'm getting."

The 23-year-old Domínguez still has big-time power potential, and defensively he's best suited to center field. For his career in the Bronx, he has an OPS+ of 93, but his 751 plate appearances have been doled out erratically across four seasons. As things stand now, he'll once again be subject to a playing-time crunch. Aaron Judge and Cody Bellinger are installed at the outfield corners, and Giancarlo Stanton, if healthy, should get much of the playing time at DH. That leaves center field for Jones or Domínguez. Other teams no doubt see that bottleneck and are seeing if Cashman and the Yankees are willing to relieve it through trade.

Lefty ace and two-time American League Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal remains far and away the top talent on the free-agent market. While the New York Mets and incumbent Los Angeles Dodgers seem like the favorites to secure his services, the San Diego Padres also have significant interest in him. That interest took the next step on Thursday with an in-person meeting, The Athletic reports. The Padres are the fourth team to meet with Skubal, who turned 30 on Friday. Previously, the Dodgers, Mets, and Toronto Blue Jays met with him.

The Padres have a pronounced need in the rotation, especially if free-agent right-hander Michael King signs elsewhere. Last winter, they also lost Dylan Cease to the Blue Jays via free agency.

The Padres and left-handed platoon hitter Gavin Sheets have agreed to a three-year, $11 million contract extension that includes two opt-outs, FanSided reports. Sheets, who'll turn 31 in April, had been slated for free agency after the upcoming season. Instead, he and the Padres will now be potentially committed through the 2029 season, depending on whether Sheets exercises any of his opt-outs. While he's not much of a hitter for average, he does draw walks and hit for power. In two seasons with San Diego, he's tallied 36 home runs and 44 doubles in 855 at-bats while seeing DH, first base, and the outfield corners.

The New York Mets have agreed to a three-year, $12 million deal with right-handed reliever Darwinzon Hernández, reports José F. Rivera.

Hernández, who turns 30 in December, hasn't pitched in MLB since 2022 and instead has revived his career with four strong seasons in Japan. Over that span for Softbank of the NPB, he's put up an ERA of 2.46 in 131 ⅔ innings with 168 strikeouts and 42 unintentional walks. Prior to rebuilding himself in Japan, Hernández had a 5.06 ERA and a 1.82 K/BB ratio over parts of four seasons with the Boston Red Sox.

#2517. Ranking the NBA's most hopeless teams: Which franchise is in the bleakest situation? And who can't fix it?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Milwaukee Bucks faced Giannis Antetokounmpo as an opponent for the first time on Wednesday, and it didn't go well. Though the final score showed only a seven-point margin, the Miami Heat led by 26 after three quarters and were never in much danger. The defeat dropped the Bucks to 1-14 on the season. The greatest player in their franchise's history now wears another jersey, and they're at the beginning of what figures to be a very long rebuild. Things are bleak.

The question here is how bleak. Milwaukee knew it would spend this season in the cellar. It probably expects to live there for a few years. But how far away from winning seriously are the Bucks really? Are they further from genuine contention than any other team in the NBA? Who, right now, has the bleakest long-term outlook?

To be clear here, we are operating in terms of championship equity. We don't care if you have a chance to be a plucky .500 team. No, the barometer we're using here is how likely each team is to reach a conference finals in the next five seasons. We're accounting not only for players on the existing roster, but long-term financial flexibility, available draft assets and the competence of the front office helming these organizations. With all of that in mind, let's rank the NBA's most hopeless long-term outlooks.

The broad sentiment following their punishment for circumventing the salary cap with Kawhi Leonard was that the Clippers faced the bleakest future in the entire NBA. That's probably overstating things slightly.

Remember, we're talking about a Los Angeles team here. Someone, inevitably, is going to want to play for them. All it takes is one player bucking the league-wide trend against superstar free agency and they're back in business. They have an owner who will spare no expense in pursuit of wins, and there's a 26-year-old All-Star in Darius Garland already on the roster. Couple that with the hope generated by No. 5 overall pick Keaton Wagler, and while the path here is extremely narrow, it exists. If the Brooklyn Nets could build a contender without draft picks in the late 2010s, it's theoretically possible for the Clippers to do the same.

Of course, the Nets weren't subject to that league-wide pivot away from free agency. They didn't have to trade picks to get Kevin Durant or Kyrie Irving in the door. It's much, much harder nowadays to import talent like that without sacrificing picks that the Clippers frankly don't have. The five first-round picks they were docked in the Leonard investigation left them fully Stepien-locked: while they will have (not especially valuable) first-round picks in odd-numbered years moving forward, they can't trade any of them yet.

There's also the reputational hit the Clippers just took. Will players interested in winning want to risk their careers on a team that cheated? Can the Clippers even appeal to such players given their asset deficit? These are going to be real hurdles. Their path to the conference finals might rely on a star who's not especially competitive. After all, anyone serious about winning could find a team closer to doing so.

They're a blank slate with one very promising prospect. Darius Acuff is putting up star box-score numbers in his rookie season. That's by no means a guarantee of future stardom, of course. He's as inefficient as you'd expect a rookie to be on this volume. He's taking more shots per game than Jalen Brunson, Tyrese Maxey or Dwyane Wade ever did over a full season. But Acuff has a path to becoming one of the NBA's best offensive point guards. These aren't totally empty calories.

There's nothing else here. No other notable prospects aside from a handful of likely long-term bench youngsters (Dylan Cardwell, Maxime Raynaud, Emanuel Sharp). Sacramento mostly controls its own picks (aside from the 2031 swap it inexplicably gave San Antonio in the DeMar DeRozan sign-and-trade), but that means less than it used to in the lottery reform era. Its books slowly clean up in the offseasons to come, with Zach LaVine and De'Andre Hunter expiring after this season and Domantas Sabonis and Malik Monk joining them in the summer of 2028, but Sacramento's forays into cap space have typically been unsuccessful. This isn't exactly a desirable destination. That's what happens when you miss the playoffs 19 times in 20 years.

That's what separates Sacramento from fellow "one possible star, otherwise blank slate" candidates like the Chicago Bulls. With the hire of Bryson Graham to run basketball operations, the Bulls at least appear to be trending towards becoming a normal organization. Normalcy has eternally eluded Sacramento. The burden of proof is on the Kings. When you've been a mess for 20 years, it's on you to prove that you've cleaned up your act. We'll trust the Kings when they've earned it and not a second sooner.

For now, they can at least start by actually keeping their success stories in the building. They've kept only one first-round pick this decade through the end of his rookie contract: Keegan Murray, who is now pretty substantially overpaid. Meanwhile, Tyrese Haliburton has blossomed into a superstar in Indiana, while their entire 2021 draft class (Davion Mitchell and Neemias Queta) now starts for Eastern Conference championship hopefuls. They had the unanimous Coach of the Year and the Executive of the Year and fired both within two years. The Kings can't help themselves.

There's far more talent in the cupboard here than in Sacramento, but the same organizational concerns apply. The Joe Dumars regime makes mistakes -- the two-year minimum for DeAndre Jordan, not waiting until after the 2025 Finals to trade Indiana its 2026 pick back, everything Shamit Dua has reported about the infamous Derik Queen trade -- that typical teams would never dream of.

There is not a discernible plan here besides, seemingly, "acquire players who can put the ball through the hoop." There are a lot of decent individual creators on this roster. None of them synergize well because so few of them can consistently make 3s and all of them are on-ball players with stylistic clashes. The Pelicans have seemingly made the determination, for instance, that Queen cannot play significant minutes alongside Zion Williamson. That's a reasonable choice... but then why is Williamson still on the team? Or, if the Pelicans view him as a fixture, why make such a risky trade for Queen in the first place?

The trickle-down effect of putting all of these dribblers on the same team is that none of them seem happy to be on it. Dejounte Murray asked for a trade. Jordan Poole is making googly eyes at the Warriors. Trey Murphy has reportedly signaled a desire to move. What is the plan here? What kind of team are the Pelicans trying to build? What do they view as their path to genuine winning?

That's what distinguishes New Orleans from Sacramento. If the Kings get a few more high draft picks and use them on players that complement Acuff, I'd see the vision. It would require Acuff becoming an All-NBA scorer and those picks hitting, but I see the sort of teams they could build, even if they're unlikely to actually do so. I have no earthly idea what the Pelicans would do with a few high picks because talent is not currently the problem. It's how they're using and nurturing it. It's just hard to envision a team with so little understanding of how to balance skill sets and bring out the best in their players making a serious playoff push. Something significant in the organization would have to change.

They're the best team on this list in the present, and they've clawed their way back to .500 after a miserable start that included leaks about the team's lack of a point guard. Again, we're dealing in upside here. That's what the Suns lack.

They control none of their own first-round picks in the seven-year tradable window except for their 2032 selection... which is frozen because they spent the 2024-25 season above the second apron. Even if they had picks, the Suns under Matt Ishbia have never displayed any discipline in using them. Ishbia traded nearly a full draft for Kevin Durant mere days after acquiring the team, spent an unprotected 2031 pick on three far lesser choices that amounted to Mark Williams and a Jusuf Nurkić cap dump, and then spent their 2033 pick as soon as they could access it to get Miles Bridges, whom they've been meaningfully better without thus far this season.

The most talented players here are all right around their physical peaks. Devin Booker is 30. Dillon Brooks turns 31 this season, and Bridges turns 29. They're going to get worse, not better, and without draft picks, their means of replacing them are minimal. Even the diamonds they've dug out of the rough are on the older side. Collin Gillespie is 27. Jordan Goodwin is 28. The truly young players, like Khaman Maluach and Rasheer Fleming, have thus far underwhelmed. The younger, star-level talent here is Jalen Green, who plays Booker's position and has been a disaster on both ends this season. Why exactly is he still starting over Gillespie? Are the Suns just trying to salvage his trade value?

Teams like the Clippers, Kings and Pelicans are at least young enough and financially flexible enough to grow. The Suns, at least from an asset and financial standpoint, are essentially all-in on a Play-In-caliber roster. That Play-In-caliber roster is going to get worse as it gets older and more expensive and, without access to top talent in the draft, replenishing it is going to be borderline impossible.

The Bucks cherry-pick traits from all of our other selections. The Clippers circumvented the cap; the Bucks are getting investigated for doing so with Gary Trent Jr. The Pelicans have a roster full of overlapping skill sets; the Bucks have a million shooting guards, which made the decision to re-sign Trent for $64 million all the stranger. The Suns don't control any of their own picks and the Bucks won't until 2031 at the earliest. The Kings have the NBA's least-successful owner in Vivek Ranadivé, while the Bucks may have the NFL's in Jimmy Haslam, though he technically won't become governor until 2028 due to Milwaukee's bizarre ownership structure (another point against them, as successful teams tend to have stable leadership rather than rotating five-year terms).

Who is going to be the best player on the team in five years? Brayden Burries is the best long-term prospect, but he profiles as more of a high-end role player. Tyler Herro was an All-Star in the sense that Norman Powell and D'Angelo Russell were All-Stars: they put up big numbers in a weak Eastern Conference. Kel'El Ware was the lottery ticket from the Giannis Antetokounmpo trade and he's been so bad that he's somehow playing less than he did on a Heat team that was trying to win. Without access to their own picks or a market that tends to draw free agents, they're basically hoping someone internal (Nate Ament? Ryan Rollins?) breaks out or that they hit on a pick far later than you should rely on.

You could argue that just by virtue of being in the Eastern Conference, the Bucks have a cleaner path to the final four than those West teams do because they don't have to worry about Victor Wembanyama or the specter of healthier versions of the Oklahoma City Thunder down the line. That's fair, but as we've seen this year, injuries loom over every season. You know what else the West has aside from those two juggernauts? The four other teams on this list. The Bucks, by a wide margin, are the most hopeless team in their own conference. They're starting from the absolute bottom.

This was potentially avoidable. Had they acted sooner and traded Antetokounmpo in 2025 when the whole world knew a deal was eventually coming, they could have secured a stronger return and set themselves up for a quicker turnaround. Alas, the Bucks chose to waive-and-stretch Damian Lillard, locking them into $22.5 million in dead money through the end of the decade so they could sign Myles Turner to a contract that is increasingly looking like $28 million or so per year in... close to dead money. Milwaukee got its championship in 2021, but at this rate, it's going to be a while before it sniffs another one.

The San Francisco 49ers have extended president of football operations and general manager John Lynch's contract, according to multiple reports. The length of the extension for Lynch, who has been with the franchise for the last 10 years, was not announced at the time of reporting.

Lynch, 55, currently presides over the NFL's best team by record. The 49ers are currently 9-1 (the Bills are the only other team with one loss) and are in position to earn the NFC's No. 1 seed with seven weeks remaining in the 2026 regular season.

The 49ers have continued to have success this season despite their usual alarming injury total. Their latest injury blow occurred during Sunday night's win over Minnesota when right tackle Colton McKivitz suffered a season-ending ankle injury.

Lynch, a Hall of Fame safety who won a Super Bowl with the Buccaneers in 2002, became the 49ers' general manager in 2017. The title was expanded to include President of Football Operations in 2023.

San Francisco has been one of the league's most successful teams since Lynch's arrival. Since 2017, the 49ers have compiled a 91-68 regular-season record and a 9-5 postseason record, including NFC titles in 2019 and 2023. The 49ers lost in the Super Bowl in both of those seasons to the Kansas City Chiefs.

One of Lynch's biggest moves this past offseason was the signing of free agent Mike Evans, who chose to sign with the 49ers instead of continuing his career with the Buccaneers. Despite injuries, Evans has been an extremely productive player this season. He caught six passes for 109 yards and a score in Sunday night's win over Minnesota.

Lynch's tenure also includes the selection of Brock Purdy with the final pick in the 2022 NFL Draft. Purdy helped lead the 49ers to the Super Bowl a year later (with help from Christian McCaffrey, who was acquired the previous season just before the trade deadline) and is now a serious MVP candidate.

One of Lynch's biggest moves in San Francisco was hiring Kyle Shanahan as coach in 2017. Shanahan's contract was extended back in September.

#2515. Luis Gil, Nolan Gorman, Trevor Larnach, more hit MLB free agency after non-tender deadline

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Friday marked the non-tender deadline in Major League Baseball. That important date on the offseason calendar is when clubs must make, or "tender," contract offers for the upcoming season to all their arbitration-eligible and pre-arbitration players on the 40-player roster. That's every player who isn't a free agent or isn't presently signed to a multi-year contract. Players who are tendered a contract by that deadline remain with their current organizations. Players who aren't offered a contract become free agents.

Most such decisions are easy and obvious. Others, however, present difficult calls for the organization because of roster crunches, crowded depth charts, or, more commonly, reluctance to retain a player as his salary rises through the arbitration process. While a number of non-tendered players are likely on their way out of the league, a select few others qualify as at least interesting to other teams and, on occasion, a few will even be coveted to varying degrees.

All that sets the stage for what follows, which is our list of the most compelling non-tendered players who are now on the market and available for hire. Let's get to it …

The 2024 AL Rookie of the Year, Gil has been injured and ineffective the last two seasons. He missed time with a shoulder issue this past season and also spent time in Triple-A. The Yankees moved him to the bullpen late in the season to see whether he could contribute that way, though Gil was unable to make a strong impression in that role. Now 28, Gil still has another three seasons of team control remaining. Whichever team signs him will be able to keep him through 2029, and that extra control, plus his Rookie of the Year pedigree, will no doubt land Gil with a new team before Opening Day.

As a 23-year-old in 2023, the infielder and former first-rounder hit 27 home runs in 119 games and looked like a future cornerstone for the Cardinals. Gorman, however, has gotten steadily worse since then thanks largely to his persistent strikeout issues. Last season, he wound up back at Triple-A for an extended stretch and didn't fare any better upon being recalled. Long-term, the Cardinals will likely look to hand the third base position to rising power prospect Jesús Báez, who was recently added to the 40-player roster. Gorman can be a plus at third and probably still get by at second, and no doubt some team will take a chance on his power.

On the downside, Larnach is a defensive minus at the corner outfield spots and probably needs to be a DH, and he's also a platoon bat. On the upside, he's been a steady producer from the left side of the plate. This past season, he put up a .352 OBP and an OPS+ of 120 for Minnesota. For his career, he has an OPS+ of 106 across parts of six MLB seasons. He out-hit his underlying indicators by a bit in 2026, but Larnach is still going to be an appealing part-time bat for some teams.

The Twins cut bait on a right-hander who's made 139 career starts for them since his 2021 big-league debut. Ober boasts a career OPS+ of 102, but that figure has slid over the last two seasons. What's also slid is Ober's fastball velocity, which may be why he's on this list. In his rookie season, he averaged a fringy 92.4 mph with his four-seamer, but last season that figure was down all the way to 88 mph. That put him in the very bottom percentile among MLB hurlers. The 31-year-old Ober still should draw some interest as a depth piece.

A platoon extraordinaire, Raley has always hit for power against righties, including 15 home runs in only 290 plate appearances against them in 2026. He's sneaky fast and a very good athlete for his size (6-foot-3 and 235 lbs.), good enough to handle the corner outfield spots competently. Raley also has first base experience and can patrol center field in a pinch. The Mariners cut him loose even though he will remain under team control through 2028. Raley's power against righties and an extra year of control could make him a solid bench option moving forward.

If you were wondering how long it would take for the pitchforks to make an appearance in Toronto, the answer was 20 games. After a promising start, the Maple Leafs have lost four in a row and six of their last seven.

One of the key factors in this early slide is the play of goaltender Sergei Bobrovsky. Who could have guessed that signing a 38-year-old goalie to a big-money contract was a bad idea? Bobrovsky ranks 62nd in the NHL with -3.68 goals saved above average, and his .881 save percentage is tied for 42nd.

It's been a concerning stretch for Bobrovsky, but he also doesn't shoulder all of the blame for this skid. The Leafs have scored just 17 goals in their last seven games, and a forward group that lacks depth has been devastated by the loss of Kirill Marchenko.

Toronto is now in jeopardy of falling behind in a competitive Atlantic Division. Only the Detroit Red Wings have been worse, and that organization has been a dumpster fire for months now. The Leafs have just a couple weeks to turn things around before Thanksgiving, a key date in the NHL season as the playoff picture begins to solidify.

#2513. Julius Randle has brutal response to Nets' blowout loss: 'One of the worst games I've ever been a part of'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Brooklyn Nets are no strangers to losing games this season, as they fell to 3-11 on Wednesday night, but in a season filled with lopsided defeats, losing by 30 points to the Chicago Bulls stood out as a new low point.

The Bulls also entered Wednesday's game at 3-10 on the season, operating as one of the league's worst teams so far, but Chicago exploded for 137 points against the Nets, with eight players reaching double figures. While Chicago's biggest issue has come on the defensive end this season, the Bulls haven't exactly been lighting opponents up offensively, sitting 23rd in the league in offensive rating.

The Nets' complete inability to put up a resistance against the Bulls rang alarm bells in Brooklyn and had veteran Julius Randle calling out his team for an "embarrassing" and "unacceptable" performance.

"I've been in the league for 13 years... that's one of the worst games I've ever been a part of."Julius Randle didn't hold back after the Nets’ 30-point loss to Bulls. 😳 pic.twitter.com/s3YQ8TxP35

"The main struggle? I don't know, that was embarrassing," Randle said after the game. "Been in the league for 13 years and that's one of the worst games I've ever been a part of. And not because of the score. You lose by 30 sometimes -- it's just a bad night -- but it's how we did it. That just, it wasn't cool. Nothing about it was cool. We gotta find a way to figure out the root of it or whatever, but that just is unacceptable."

Considering Randle has been on his fair share of bad basketball teams over his career in Los Angeles, New Orleans and New York, that's saying something.

There are five teams that have separated themselves from the pack at the bottom of the NBA in terms of defense and the Nets are one of them with a 119.0 defensive rating (26th in the league). No one expected much of Brooklyn on that end of the floor with the roster they've assembled, but it's one thing to have lesser talent on the defensive end; it's another to combine that with a general lack of effort.

This early in the season, the latter is a much larger concern and the Nets have now given up at least 124 points in five of their last six games. If they were able to shrug off some of those lopsided losses to quality teams as life in the NBA, Wednesday was proof that their problems extend far beyond just some schedule losses.

Giving up 137 to a Bulls team that's been similarly bad this year is, in Randle's words, unacceptable. The concern is that no one in Brooklyn, including Randle, seems quite sure what the exact problem is or how to fix it.

#2512. Commanders vs. Bengals prediction: Cincinnati looks to extend lead in AFC North in 'MNF' matchup

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

In the Week 11 edition of "Monday Night Football," the Washington Commanders play host to the Cincinnati Bengals. Washington enters this game having won two of its last three since returning from the bye. The Commanders scored a come-from-behind victory over the division rival New York Giants last week, keeping their hopes alive in the NFC East in the process. Jayden Daniels and Co. are still just 3-5-1 on the season, but given the relative weaknesses of the NFC East, they can count themselves as divisional contenders if they can string together some wins over the next few weeks.

Cincinnati enters this game at 7-2 and in first place in the AFC North. The Bengals are red hot, having won five in a row while scoring at least 31 points in each of those contests. Joe Burrow, Ja'Marr Chase, Tee Higgins and Chase Brown are tearing holes in opposing defenses, and Cincinnati's own defense is much improved since last year. The Bengals can open up a two-game lead in the division with a win on Monday night.

Will Washington secure back-to-back wins for the first time this season, or will Cincinnati keep rolling? We'll find out soon enough as kickoff is approaching. Before we break down the matchup, here's a look at how you can watch the game.

Joe Burrow enters this game as the MVP favorite and the hottest quarterback in the NFL. Burrow is leading the NFL in completions, completion percentage, touchdowns, first downs, yards per game, success rate, passer rating and QBR while ranking second in EPA per play, according to Tru Media.

Over the last five games, he is practically touching the surface of the sun, completing 77.6% of his passes at an average of 8.9 yards per attempt, with 20 touchdown passes and three interceptions. He's totaled at least four scores in each of those five games, tying a league-record streak. During that stretch, his 0.42 EPA per dropback mark is more than 50% better than the second-place player, Trevor Lawrence (0.26), per Tru Media. He is shredding every single coverage with ease.

Ja'Marr Chase is on nearly as much of a heater as is Burrow. Chase has a 43-666-4 receiving line since the Bengals' Week 5, and he's recorded at least 10 catches for 141 yards in each of the Bengals' last three games. Last week, he went off for 231 yards against the division rival Pittsburgh Steelers — the fourth 200-plus-yard game of his career. The Commanders, needless to say, do not have anybody who has a hope of guarding him.

The Commies have been known to double opposing No. 1 wideouts more often than other teams this season, but even doing that might not necessarily be wise because Tee Higgins is playing the best football of his career as well. Higgins has a 53-824-6 receiving line so far this season, as he's averaging a career-best 91.6 receiving yards per game. He's been a bit quieter than Chase over the last two weeks, but he still has 10 grabs for 88 yards and two touchdowns in that time. His size and physicality make him a nightmare matchup for any cornerback, especially with Burrow playing as well as he is at the moment.

Meanwhile, the Commanders have allowed the NFL's fourth-most completions to tight ends so far this season, as well as the second-most yards and touchdowns. That could open up opportunities for Mike Gesicki and/or Drew Sample, though Gesicki is obviously the bigger receiving threat of the two.

Washington has actually been somewhat solid against the run this season, allowing only 4.0 yards per carry. Opposing offensive lines have cleared the way for only 1.08 yards before contact per rush, according to Tru Media, and the second-level defenders have limited rushers to the third-lowest broken tackle rate in the league.

However, the Bengals basically only run the ball as an occasional changeup, with Chase Brown and Samaje Perine acting as receivers nearly as often as they do runners. Even if the Commanders shut down the run game, it seems unlikely to matter much to Cincinnati's offensive success. Everything runs through Burrow, Chase and Higgins.

Jayden Daniels has been efficient since his return from his elbow injury, completing 67.3% of his passes at an average of 7.6 yards per attempt. He has seven touchdowns and two interceptions, along with 180 rushing yards and two touchdowns on 30 carries across five games during which the Commanders have compiled a 2-2-1 record. Daniels hasn't been particularly explosive during that stretch, but he has kept the chains moving for the most part, and the Commies have been able to stay in games against the Giants (twice) and Eagles while losing by only one score to the 49ers and Rams.

Without Terry McLaurin, Daniels' top targets are Stefon Diggs, rookie Antonio Williams, Treylon Burks, Van Jefferson and tight end Chig Okonkwo.

Diggs is mostly a short-area target who splits his time between the perimeter and the slot. He works the underneath zones as Daniels tries to matriculate the ball down the field. Williams has become a bigger part of the rotation in recent weeks but hasn't really popped off that much despite the increase in role. Burks is a rotational deep threat who has seen his snap share increase since McLaurin went down, while Jefferson works in behind each of the top three. Okonkwo is a short-area chain mover similar to Diggs, but with perhaps more run-after-catch ability relative to his position.

The Bengals are surprisingly 12th in the NFL in net yards allowed per attempt (which accounts for yardage lost due to sacks), and they have allowed only 11 passing touchdowns so far this season. They have a solid enough group of defensive backs, including one star in DJ Turner II, and their tackling has improved significantly on the second level of the defense this year.

The Commanders don't have much of a run game to speak of, what with their stable of backs combining to average just 3.7 yards per carry this season. They'll get Jacory Croskey-Merritt back on Monday night, but even he is only at 3.6 yards per carry this season. He's likely to split work with both Rachaad White and Austin Ekeler, each of whom is better in the passing game than they are when running the football.

With big Dexter Lawrence in the middle of the defensive line, it could be difficult for Washington to get anything going on the ground, even though the Bengals have actually been hit for 5.0 yards per opponent rush attempt so far this season. Lawrence has near single-handedly taken over a few games or stretches of possessions, even if teams like the Dolphins, Titans and Falcons have been able to find holes on the ground.

The current version of the Commanders does not have the firepower to keep up with the Joe Burrow, Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins show. I'm not sure any version of the Commanders ever did, but even in winning two of their last three games, they haven't exactly looked impressive. The Bengals, meanwhile, are putting on an aerial assault for the ages every week. Pick: Bengals 31, Commanders 20

#2510. NBA's eight biggest disappointments through one month: Injury bug, same old East and an underwhelming champ

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

We're roughly one month into the 2026-27 NBA season, and things are going pretty well in certain respects. Luka Dončić and the Lakers are off to a hot start in Los Angeles. Victor Wembanyama and the Spurs have picked up right where they left off after last season's Finals trip. And the Celtics are battling the new-look Sixers at the top of the Eastern Conference.

In other areas, things are going … not so well. Below are the eight biggest disappointments so far this season.

There have been so many players impacted by various injuries that it's almost hard to keep track. Jalen Duren (hamstring) has missed almost the entire season in Detroit. Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody are still recovering from knee injuries and have yet to play for Golden State, while Steph Curry is now out with an abdominal tear and Kristaps Porziņģis stepped away from basketball. After sitting out all of last season with an Achilles tear, Tyrese Haliburton is currently dealing with a hamstring issue. Brandon Ingram (Achilles) hasn't made his debut for the Clippers. Austin Reaves is out with a heel injury. Anthony Edwards underwent knee surgery and will miss a chunk of time for the Wolves, and it seems unlikely that Donte DiVincenzo (Achilles) will play this season, even though he remains hopeful that he will. Paolo Banchero remains sidelined with an ankle sprain. Ja Morant is out with a hamstring strain. Ben Simmons didn't play a single game for the Kings before tearing his Achilles. Kawhi Leonard (knee) is once again on the shelf in Toronto. And the reeling Jazz are without Jaren Jackson Jr (knee), Lauri Markkanen (hand) and Jusuf Nurkic (toe).

It's all a huge bummer for the players, their teams and fans of hoops in general. But no team has been hurt more on the injury front than the Thunder.

The disappointment here is how unkind fate has been to OKC. The Thunder were close to fully healthy when the season started — and then far from it not long after it began. When OKC beat the Spurs in San Antonio in the season opener — after losing four of five regular season games to them last season, as well as falling to the Spurs in the Western Conference Finals — it felt like a statement that the Thunder were back and we were in for an epic battle between the two teams over who would rule the West.

And then all of that was stripped away. Just three games into the season, Jalen Williams — who missed much of last season due to injury — suffered a gruesome fall and had to undergo surgery for a fractured fibula as well as reconstruction of ankle ligaments. In that same fateful game, Cason Wallace tore his labrum and later had shoulder surgery. They haven't been officially ruled out, but if either of them plays basketball again this season, it will be a surprise. Making matters worse, Chet Holmgren tore a tendon in his knee and "underwent a biological treatment" to address it. He'll miss approximately two months, but the Thunder do expect him to return. That's what passes for good news in OKC these days.

The Thunder are — or were — the deepest team in the NBA. That's a credit to what Sam Presti built. But even OKC has its limits. Losing three of five starters is tough to overcome, even when you're led by the reigning back-to-back MVP in Shai Gilgeous-Alexander. That doesn't mean the Thunder (currently 9-6 and eighth in the West) can't still make a deep playoff run, but the odds of them doing so — and of them fighting the Spurs all season for the top spot — got a lot longer.

We were told that this was finally the season that the East returned to its former glory. We were told that the conference would be loaded. We were wrong. (Full disclosure while putting a palm to my face: I might have done some of that telling.)

Through the first month, the East has been mostly underwhelming. Eight of the 15 teams are below .500. The conference has a combined 17-37 record against the West. Only one of the top seven teams in net rating — the Celtics — plays in the East. Five of the top six teams by point differential play in the West.

The defending champion Knicks are 8-6. The Cavaliers, who made it to last season's Eastern Conference Finals and had championship aspirations of their own, are 8-8. The Magic, Raptors and Pacers — who currently occupy the eight, nine and 10 seeds — all have losing records. By contrast, the worst play-in team in the West right now is Golden State at 8-7. That record would be good enough for the seven seed if they played in the East.

But maybe we shouldn't be surprised. Since the 1999-2000 season, the West has had the better overall record in all but three campaigns. Maybe next year the East will finally snap out of its funk, but don't bet on it.

The Jazz just picked up back-to-back road wins in L.A. over the Lakers and Clippers, but that doesn't begin to dig them out of the deep hole they've made for themselves. The Jazz were gearing up to be competitive in the West this season. So much for that. Like the Thunder, injuries have not been kind to them. Nurkic has yet to play a single game this season, while Markkanen and JJJ have missed significant time with maladies of their own. What looked like a formidable frontcourt has been decimated.

Still, it's hard to believe how bad the Jazz have been in pretty much every facet. Their first win came in the second game of the season, a one-point squeaker over the Pelicans. It took until mid-November to end an ugly 12-game losing streak and pick up their second and third wins. They're 25th in net rating and point differential. The season has barely begun, and it's already basically wait until next year for the Jazz.

The NBA panicked and tried to solve for a problem that wasn't actually an issue, except for a small fragment of people who care more about optics than the product itself. And so the league enacted lottery reform and the new 3-2-1 system was put in place. This was ostensibly designed to prevent tanking, incentivize winning and bring greater parity to the league. Oops.

The Hornets, Wizards, Bulls, Nets and Bucks are all well underwater in the East. The Pelicans and Clippers are drowning in the West, while the Kings and Jazz are even worse. What the league failed to account for is that some of these teams are just organically bad — and now they will have decreased odds at getting better.

Under the old system, the Grizzlies would be pretty thrilled to see the Jazz struggling since Memphis has Utah's first-round pick in the upcoming draft as part of the JJJ trade. Alas, after making that move, the league changed the rules, which means the Grizzlies can pick no higher than sixth now as a consequence of the new system preventing a team from picking in the top five in three consecutive drafts. Since the Jazz picked in the top five in each of the last two drafts, that means the Grizzlies are now out of luck with that Utah pick this time around. Womp, womp for them.

And on top of it all, fans of bad teams were robbed of the entertaining-in-its-own-way race to the bottom to maximize lottery odds, giving supporters a small silver lining in the otherwise gray clouds of their season. RIP Tank Watch.

When aren't the Kings disappointing? Aside from their unsightly 1-13 record, the Sacramento front office continues to make baffling decisions. The Kings originally acquired Nique Clifford from the Thunder for a Spurs 2027 first-round pick. Sacramento held onto Clifford for 83 games — choosing to bury him on the bench this season and play him barely six minutes per game — before shipping him back to the Thunder for two second-round picks.

So the Thunder ended up with the player and a first and the Kings ended up with two seconds.

One of these organizations is savvy and opportunistic, and the other is the Kings. It's a miracle they nailed the Darius Acuff pick.

Oof. It has not been a good season to date for Bridges. After going cold to begin their first-round playoff series against the Hawks, Bridges found his form and played well, helping the Knicks go on an epic run that ended with New York's first championship in 53 years.

If that hope was that Bridges would snap out of his early-season funk in similar fashion, the Knicks seem somewhat less patient these days. While head coach Mike Brown has insisted that Bridges is a starter, he has sometimes hedged his bets in crucial situations, going with Landry Shamet or Deuce McBride over Bridges when things get tight and the Knicks need more reliable offense on the floor.

Through 14 games, Bridges is averaging 7.5 points, 3.6 rebounds and 2.1 assists on 40.2/28.9/75 shooting splits. It's the lowest scoring output and the worst shooting numbers of his career. As a result, his minutes have dipped to 25.6 per contest. That's also a career low. Bridges is still a plus defender. And he's only 30. The Knicks obviously hope he'll figure it out, as he has in the past. If not, his new four-year, $150 million extension that kicked in this season will start to look worrisome.

Why are we still subjected to … [motions at everything below in the most pejorative fashion possible] ... this?

ALL 30 TEAM COURTS FOR @EMIRATES NBA CUP 2026 pic.twitter.com/RgBqe1VJCB

Why can't whoever came up with the gorgeous GTA VI crossover court in Miami be in charge of the Cup floors instead?

The Miami Heat are rolling out the “Vice City” hardwood 😮‍💨👏(via @MiamiHEAT) pic.twitter.com/AFcyK2akaV

Respecting the Cup would be so much easier if they'd give us more of this. Maybe they could dream up some sweet new jerseys while they're at it.

#2506. NBA rumors: Suitors emerging for Dejounte Murray, demand for Anthony Davis and more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 NBA season is barely a month old and trade season won't officially begin until December 15 when players signed this summer are eligible to be moved, but that doesn't stop the rumor machine from churning in the Association.

The first 15 games of the season have been enough for some teams to learn the harsh truth about not being a contender this year, while others are off to surprisingly good starts that could turn them into midseason buyers. That's how the trade market starts to take shape, and with a trade request already made in New Orleans by Dejounte Murray and a handful of expiring contracts known to be open to moving, we can start piecing together an early look at what trade season may look like.

The one unknown this season is how the league's lottery reform will affect the in-season trade market. Fewer teams will have incentive to completely bottom out, but even with teams not trying to sell everything off, there will still be enough teams trying to buy to create a market.

On Thursday, we got a fresh batch of rumors, starting with some updates on potential suitors for Murray after being sent home by the Pelicans.

Murray makes $32.8 million this year and has a player option for $30.8 million next year that he will almost assuredly pick up. That means he's not exactly a coveted asset, and even for teams with a potential need at point guard, so far no one seems to be jumping at the opportunity to trade for the disgruntled Pelicans guard.

Two teams that were quickly connected as potential destinations for Murray were the Suns and the Heat, both with glaring point guard needs and a desire to contend this season. However, neither team is desperate to make a move right now, according to Jake Fischer in the latest Stein Line newsletter.

Murray and Klutch Sports see Phoenix as a good landing spot, but the Suns view center as a bigger need than point guard and would demand that the Pelicans send back draft capital to take on Murray's salary, Fischer reports. Miami, meanwhile, has shown little appetite for Murray and he is not expected to be one of its trade targets because of his player option for next season that would severely limit their ability to retool the roster around Giannis Antetokounmpo.

With the two most obvious potential suitors for Murray not exactly showing a lot of excitement for bringing him in, it seems likely that Murray's trade request and absence from the Pelicans will extend for quite some time and could last all the way to the trade deadline.

The Washington Wizards are 5-11 to start the season, which makes it increasingly unlikely they will be trying to work out a long-term extension for Davis. The early returns on Washington's commitment to Trae Young have not been good, and if the Wizards are looking to acquire some assets this season, Davis makes the most sense as an expiring contract.

On the latest episode of the Hoop Collective, ESPN's Brian Windhorst offered an update on Davis' market and desires for his next contract.

"I think people have demand for Anthony Davis," Windhorst said. "They just don't want to give him a max extension, and I don't think he's looking for a max extension, but I do think he's looking for a lot of money."

That's not exactly groundbreaking information and any team exploring a trade for Davis will want to know what, exactly, he's looking for in his next contract. Below the max is a start, but teams are growing wary of giving out massive money to aging stars in the second apron era. Davis brings an additional level of risk to any long-term contract discussions with his injury history.

That said, he has been quite good this season -- averaging 24.6 points and 10.1 rebounds per game on solid efficiency -- and the Wizards should be shopping him to teams desperate for a center upgrade. If Phoenix is less interested in a point guard but has an appetite for a star center, perhaps the Suns could be a trade partner to offload Jalen Green's contract -- to be clear, that's not a rumor, just connecting dots between a few recent rumors.

Everything with Davis' market will come down to what Davis and Rich Paul tell teams about what they want his next contract to look like.

With Murray on the block and the Pelicans at 5-11, it's fair to wonder (again) if some of New Orleans' more intriguing players could find their way onto the trade market.

The player most teams around the league covet in New Orleans is Trey Murphy III. Even though he's in the midst of a slow start to the season and currently dealing with knee tendonitis, other teams still covet his potential as a star on the wing given his abilities as a scorer and defender. The Pelicans also believe strongly in Murphy's upside, and unfortunately for other teams, Fischer reports Murphy -- unlike Murray -- has no desire to make a trade request.

As such, he's going to be quite expensive to pry from the Pelicans, who "remain reluctant" to discuss trades for Murphy. Given he's their best potential trade chip, that's probably a wise approach, and New Orleans will hope some hopeful contender is desperate enough to give up a haul of assets before they consider moving him.

#2505. DK Metcalf will not be suspended by the NFL after getting ejected during Steelers' loss to Eagles

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The NFL will not suspend DK Metcalf for his actions during the Pittsburgh Steelers' recent loss to the Philadelphia Eagles, according to a report from ESPN's Adam Schefter. Metcalf was ejected late in the third quarter after committing his second unsportsmanlike conduct penalty.

During his Monday media availability, Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy said that he and Metcalf spoke about the situation, calling the conversations "productive." He added that any additional discipline ffrom the Steelers would be kept internal.

"Life's about learning situations," McCarthy said. "I do believe in second chances. I will judge him based on my personal interaction with him. I did appreciate the way he communicated today."

Sunday's ejection marks Metcalf's third ejection in his eight-season career. Metcalf was also suspended for the final two games of the 2025 regular season after getting into a physical confrontation with a Lions fan. He returned for the playoffs but dropped a key pass early in Pittsburgh's eventual 30-6 loss to Houston.

Metcalf was already fined earlier this year for an unsportsmanlike penalty during Pittsburgh's Week 4 loss to the Cleveland Browns. It was the latest in a series of fines Metcalf has accrued during his NFL career.

Metcalf's fines have totaled a whopping $245,647, according to Spotrac. This does not include an additional $555,555 fine attached to his two-game suspension for the Lions fan altercation.

While his actions have hurt his wallet, his lack of production has hurt the Steelers on the field.  Outside of his 11-catch performance against the Buccaneers in Week 6, Metcalf has had over five receptions in a game just once this season. He's had just six catches in Pittsburgh's last four games. He had one catch for just two yards before being ejected from Sunday's game after trying to poke Eagles defensive back Cooper DeJean in the eye.

Metcalf, 28, hasn't been the same player since he signed a four-year, $132 million contract with Pittsburgh shortly after he was traded from Seattle. Last year (his first in Pittsburgh), Metcalf caught 59 passes for 850 yards, which were both career lows. His six touchdown catches tied a career low.

His lack of production and on-field issues have led to questions about his future with the Steelers. For now, all that is known is that Metcalf will be available for Friday's big showdown between Pittsburgh and Denver.

#2498. MLB rumors: Logan Webb trade possible for Giants, Freddy Peralta market picking up steam, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The uncertain 2026-27 Major League Baseball offseason is fully underway. The ongoing CBA negotiations and the near certainty of an owner-implemented lockout on Dec. 2 loom over all, and it may indeed mean a flurry of trades and free agent signings leading up to that date. That was certainly the case leading up to the last lockout of 2021-22, and this time around we've already seen some leading examples.

Thanks to that prospect of a hastened pace, offseason rumors are flowing. Speaking of which, we'll be here each day to round up what's out there. You can find Saturday's supply just below.

Will the San Francisco Giants trade their ace this offseason? That's a reasonable question to ask now that FanSided is reporting that the Giants are open to trade discussions regarding veteran right-hander Logan Webb. No doubt, Webb would be a coveted presence on the offseason market.

Webb, who just recently turned 30, endured a bit of a down 2026 on the run-prevention front, but the overall body of work remains very strong. For his career, the three-time All-Star has a career ERA+ of 115 with three top-10 finishes in the American League Cy Young vote. In three of the past four seasons, he's topped 200 innings.

Webb is under contract through 2028, and that extra year of team control makes him even more of an alluring trade target for contenders in need of rotation upgrades.

Freddy Peralta, who'll be going into his age-31 season in 2027, is one of the strongest free-agent starting pitchers on the market not named Tarik Skubal. As such, there's healthy interest in his services. The Tampa Bay Rays, the Chicago White Sox, the San Diego Padres, the Toronto Blue Jays, and two presently unknown clubs all have significant interest in signing Peralta, the Athletic reports.

Peralta, coming off three straight seasons for the Milwaukee Brewers in which he topped 30 starts and 200 strikeouts, wasn't himself with the New York Mets for the first half-plus of 2027. However, after a deadline trade to the Rays, he made some adjustments and re-established himself as a highly useful starter. The market's going to reflect his rediscovered form.

Right-hander Hiromi Itoh, who's seeking to make the leap from Japan to MLB, was recently in Chicago to visit the Cubs or the White Sox, ESPN reports. Both Windy City squads are in need of pitching help, and Itoh would certainly help them on that front.

The 29-year-old Itoh ranked 26th on CBS Sports' offseason list of the top free agents in the current class. Here's part of our write-up:

"A down 2026 season took some of the shine off Itoh, who won the 2025 Eiji Sawamura Award (Japan's Cy Young equivalent) after throwing 196 ⅔ innings with a 2.52 ERA. To be sure, Itoh pitched well in 2026 (3.18 ERA in 172 ⅔ innings), but he was not as consistently dominant as in the past. The 5-foot-9 right-hander is a seven-pitch pitcher with a low-90s fastball and the usual array of secondary pitches (sinker, cutter, curveball, slider, sweeper, splitter), none of which stands out as a plus offering. Itoh has thrown at least 150 innings in each of the last six seasons. He's seen as a crafty back-end starter in MLB, or perhaps even a reliever (Itoh sat 96 mph out of the bullpen in the World Baseball Classic). The Hokkaido Nippon Ham Fighters are expected to post Itoh, who turned 29 in August, this winter."

The Cubs have a lot of uncertainty in the rotation, while the White Sox still need help even after adding Dustin May this offseason.

The New York Mets retained the services of first baseman Mark Vientos leading up to the recent non-tender deadline despite his pattern of decline over the last two seasons. Now, Vientos could be on the move. The soon-to-be 27-year-old has been the subject of trade inquiries, The Athletic reports.

While Vientos is coming off a highly disappointing 2026 season, he still has power potential and in his semi-recent past a 2024 campaign in which he hit 27 home runs in 111 games. All of that makes Vientos a fairly compelling change-of-scenery possibility, and the Mets may seek to make that happen this winter.
